title: 11  Minimization of DFAs
text:
11.1 The minimum DFA (formal definition)
In this chapter we see minimization algorithms for DFAs, that is algorithms that given as input a DFA A find the1 DFA B with the smallest number of states possible s.t. \mathscr{L}(B)=\mathscr{L}(A).
Notice that the minimal DFA accepting a language is unique (up to isomorphism), but in general there is not a unique minimum NFA accepting a language.
One interesting property of DFAs is that for DFAs an analogue of the previous Example 11.1 cannot happen! All minimum DFA accepting a given language are isomorphic. For this reason we refer to the minimum DFA (up to isomorphism) accepting a given language.
Given a DFA A=(Q,\Sigma,\{q_0\},F,\delta), to find the minimum DFA for \mathscr{L}(A), first remove all unreachable states from the initial state q_0: those are clearly redundant. No computation starting at q_0 can ever visit an unreachable state, so removing such states leaves \mathscr{L}(A) unchanged. For simplicity of notation let’s call again A the DFA obtained after removing all those unreachable states.
We say that two states q,q'\in Q are equivalent (q\sim q') if 
\mathscr{L}(A_q)=\mathscr{L}(A_{q'})\ ,
\tag{11.1}
where A_q is the DFA obtained from A marking the initial state of A as a normal state and taking as new initial state q (and similarly for A_{q'}). If q\not\sim q', that is if \mathscr{L}(A_q)\neq\mathscr{L}(A_{q'}), we say that q and q' are distinguishable.
If q and q' are equivalent, then they behave in the same way w.r.t. accepting or not words and hence can be identified. That is, if in A the states q and q' are equivalent, then q' can be safely removed re-routing all incoming transitions to q (and make q the initial state if q' was the initial state).
Let [q] be the set of all states equivalent to q, that is 
[q]=\{q'\in Q :\mathscr{L}(A_q)=\mathscr{L}(A_{q'})\}\ .
 Let \min(A)=(Q',\Sigma,I',F',\delta') be the DFA that has
It turns out that \min(A) is the minimum DFA equivalent to A, i.e. A and \min(A) accept the same language and \min(A) has the smallest number of states possible among the DFAs equivalent to A.
We don’t see the proof of this result in this course (it is a consequence of the Myhill-Nerode Theorem), but we leave as an exercise to check the first part of it.
The main difficulty in computing the minimum DFA is to compute Q', that is the partition of the states of Q induced by the equivalence. In the next couple of sections we see two algorithms to compute \min(A).

title: 11  Minimization of DFAs
text:
Q'=\{[q] :q\in Q\},
I'=\{[q_0]\}, where q_0 is the initial state of A,
F'=\{[q] :q\in F\}, where F are the final states of A,
\delta':Q'\times \Sigma\to Q' where 
\delta'([q],\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}})=[\delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}})]\ .




Theorem 11.1 For each DFA A, the DFA \min(A) constructed above has the following properties:

\mathscr{L}(A)=\mathscr{L}(\min(A));
no DFA with strictly less states than \min(A) accepts \mathscr{L}(A);
all DFAs with the same number of states as \min(A) and accepting \mathscr{L}(A) are isomorphic to \min(A).








John R. Myhill Sr. (1923-1987)





Anil Nerode (1932-)



Exercise 11.1 Prove that for DFAs A and \min(A) as defined above, A and \min(A) accept the same language.








Tip



Finding a minimum DFA equivalent to a given DFA is a different task than, given a DFA show that it is minimal. For example, if you just want to prove minimality sometimes it is easier/faster to construct a fooling set (see Section 14.1).

title: 11  Minimization of DFAs
text:
11.2 Moore’s minimization algorithm





Edward F. Moore (1925-2003)


For every q\in Q we want to compute [q]. Moore’s minimization algorithm is a partition refinement algorithm that computes the equivalence \sim starting with a very coarse partition of Q and then refining it until reaching \sim.

Exercise 11.2 (🌱 Trivial cases) Given a DFA A=(Q,\Sigma,I,F,\delta), what is the minimum DFA equivalent to A if

F=\emptyset?
F=Q?


In the rest of the section consider fixed a DFA A=(Q,\Sigma,\{q_0\},F,\delta) to minimize and assume \emptyset\subsetneq F\subsetneq Q (otherwise as seen in Exercise 11.2 the minimization is trivial), also assume that all states in Q are reachable from q_0.
The idea to find the equivalence classes of \sim, that is all states that are distinguishable from each other, is to start approximating \sim with finer and finer partitions corresponding to states distinguishable with words up to length 0,1,2,\dots
Formally, let \mathscr{L}(A)_{\leqslant k} be the words of length at most k accepted by A. We say that q and q' are k-equivalent (q\sim_k q') if

\mathscr{L}(A_q)_{\leqslant k}=\mathscr{L}(A_{q'})_{\leqslant k}\ ,
\tag{11.2}
where A_q is the DFA obtained from A marking the initial state of A as a normal state and taking as new initial state q (and similarly for A_{q'}). Similarly as before let [q]_{k}=\{q'\in Q:q'\sim_k q\}, that is [q]_{k} is the set of all states k-equivalent to q.
The equivalence classes of \sim_0 give a partition 
\pi_0=\{[q]_0:q\in Q\}\ .

What is \pi_0? The states that can be distinguished with words of length 0 (that is \varepsilon), in other words the final vs the non-final states. That is \pi_0=\{F,Q\setminus F\}.
Then we want to compute \pi_k=\{[q]_k:q\in Q\} for k=1,2,3,\dots

Exercise 11.3 Show that for each k, the partition \pi_{k+1} is a refinement of the partition \pi_k.

At each step the new partitions get finer and finer (by the exercise Exercise 11.3 above), and since the finest possible partition of Q is the one that has each vertex separately, the process must stabilize, that is there must exist a k s.t. \pi_k=\pi_{k+1}. This partition is the one we want, the one corresponding to the states of \min(A).

Theorem 11.2 If \pi_k=\pi_{k+1}, then \pi_k=\{[q]:q\in Q\}.

The idea of the algorithm is hence to compute the equivalence classes of \sim_0, \sim_1, etc. When it stabilizes this gives the equivalence classes of \sim. The following exercise shows a way to compute \sim_{k+1} from \sim_k.

Exercise 11.4 Show that q\sim_{k+1}q' if and only if q\sim_k q' and for each \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\in \Sigma, \delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}})\sim_k \delta(q',\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}).

Let \Sigma=\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s_1}},\dots,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s_\ell}}\} and let Q=\{1,\dots,n\}. We see a partition over Q as a vector \pi\in\{1,\dots,k\}^n where all the numbers between 1 and k appear at least once in \pi. Two states q and q' are in the same set of the partition if and only if \pi[q]=\pi[q'].

Example 11.2 If n=5 the vector \pi=(1,2,3,1,3) gives the partition where the vertices 1 and 4 are in the same set, no other vertex is in the same set with 2, and 3 and 5 are in the same set.

The first partition \pi_0 of Q is given by accepting and non-accepting states:

\pi_0=(b_1,\dots,b_n)\ ,
 where b_i=1 if q_i\in F and otherwise b_i=2.
In this section we use a couple of non-standard notations. For a partition \pi of the vertices of Q and q\in Q,

let \pi[q] be the unique set in \pi containing q.
let the signature of q be s[q,\pi]=(\pi[q],\pi[\delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s_1}})],\dots,\pi[\delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s_\ell}})]), that is s[q,\pi] is a vector containing as first entry the label of the block of \pi containing q, and then the names of the sets in \pi containing the vertices \delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s_1}}),\dots,\delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s_\ell}}).

If s[q,\pi]\neq s[q',\pi] it means that either q and q' do not belong to the same set of \pi or that there exist a symbol \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s_i}}\in \Sigma s.t. \delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s_i}}) and \delta(q',\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s_i}}) do not belong to the same set of \pi. In either case q and q' cannot be equivalent.
The idea is to keep refining the partition using the signature to mark states that cannot be equivalent until the partition stabilizes. When the partition does not change anymore we found the partition induced by \sim, and stop the procedure.


\begin{algorithm} \caption{Computing the refined partition $\pi'$ from $\pi$} \begin{algorithmic} \ForAll{$q \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$} \State $s[q,\pi] \gets (\pi[q],\, \pi[\delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s_1}})],\, \ldots,\, \pi[\delta(q, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s_\ell}})])$ \EndFor \State compute the permutation $\sigma$ that sorts the states according to $s$ \State $i \gets 1$ \State $\pi'[\sigma(1)] \gets i$ \ForAll{$q \in \{2,\ldots,n\}$} \If{$s[\sigma(q),\pi] \ne s[\sigma(q-1),\pi]$} \State $i \gets i + 1$ \EndIf \State $\pi'[\sigma(q)] \gets i$ \EndFor \Return $\pi'$ \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}

title: 11  Minimization of DFAs
text:
11.3 Minimization Brzozowski-style
There is a very neat way to compute the minimum DFA equivalent to a given one due to Brzozowski. He noticed that to compute the minimum DFA equivalent to a given one you only need to know the determinization construction (from Theorem 9.2) and how to construct a DFA for the reverse language (that is inverting the direction of the transitions and exchanging the role of initial and final states).


We already saw some results by Brzozowski’s in Section 8.2.
Given an NFA A, let D(A) the DFA computed using the powerset construction from the proof of Theorem 9.2 without writing down states unreachable from the initial one.
Given a DFA A=(Q,\Sigma,\{q_0\},F,\delta), let R(A) be the following NFA: R(A)=(Q,\Sigma,F,\{q_0\},\delta'), where for each \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\in \Sigma and q,q'\in Q, (q',\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}},q)\in \delta' if and only if \delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}})=q'. In other words, R(A) is the same as A but with the directions of the transitions reversed and with final and initial states exchanged. We have that R(A) accepts the language \mathscr{L}(A)^R (this was one of the NFAs you were asked to construct in Exercise 9.5).

Theorem 11.3 (Brzozowski’s minimization algorithm) Given a DFA A without unreachable states, the minimum DFA accepting \mathscr{L}(A)^R is D(R(A)). And hence, as a consequence, the minimum DFA equivalent to A is D(R(D(R(A)))).

We don’t see the proof of this result and only leave a special case as an exercise.

Exercise 11.6 Show that if all states of A are reachable from the initial state and R(A) is a DFA, then it is minimum.


Exercise 11.7 Give an example of DFA A where the running time of the algorithm given by Theorem 11.3 is exponential in the number of states of A.

 In Exercise 10.3 you constructed a DFA A accepting L. Check whether the A you constructed is minimal using the technique of Theorem 11.3.

title: 12  Regular expressions
text:
12.1 Language described by a regular expression
In this chapter we define regular expressions, which informally give a way to describe algebraically all the languages for which we were able to write DFAs/NFAs. If you ever used the Linux command grep you have already used regular expressions (but with a different syntax than the one we use here).
Given an alphabet \Sigma,1 consider the language \Sigma\cup \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{(}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)}}, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\cdot}}, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{+}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\phantom{}^*}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\varepsilon}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\emptyset}}\}. The language of regular expressions over \Sigma is defined as follows:
To avoid writing unnecessary parentheses the \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\phantom{}^*}} by convention has stronger precedence than \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\cdot}}, which, in turn, is stronger than \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{+}}. Moreover, the \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\cdot}} is often omitted (as it is often omitted multiplication in arithmetic expressions).
What is the semantics of a regular expression? To each regular expression r over an alphabet \Sigma we associate a language \mathscr{L}(r)\subseteq \Sigma^* as follows:
For a regular expression r, we say that r describes the language \mathscr{L}(r), in the sense that r describes a way to construct \mathscr{L}(r) from very simple languages (\emptyset,\{\varepsilon\},\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\}) using unions, concatenations and Kleene stars.

title: 12  Regular expressions
text:
\mathscr{L}(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\emptyset}})=\emptyset;
\mathscr{L}(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\varepsilon}})=\{\varepsilon\};
\mathscr{L}(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}})=\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\}, for each symbol \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\in \Sigma;
if r and r' are regular expressions, then \mathscr{L}(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{(}}r\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)+(}}r'\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)}})=\mathscr{L}(r)\cup \mathscr{L}(r');
if r and r' are regular expressions, then \mathscr{L}(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{(}}r\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)\cdot(}}r'\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)}})=\mathscr{L}(r)\cdot\mathscr{L}(r');
if r is a regular expression, then \mathscr{L}(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{(}}r\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)^*}})=\mathscr{L}(r)^*.


Exercise 12.1 What is \mathscr{L}(r) when r is the regular expression in Example 12.1? Describe it using the standard logic notation to describe sets.

The language of all words over \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\} of even length;

The language of all words over the usual English keyboard symbols that are valid email addresses.



Exercise 12.3 (Equivalence of regular expressions) This exercise is about checking the equivalence of two regular expressions using simple algebraic manipulations. We say that two regular expressions p,q are equivalent (p\equiv q) if the languages represented by p and q (resp. \mathscr{L}(p) and \mathscr{L}(q)) are the same.
Show that for all regular expressions p, q, and r:

(p+q)^* \equiv p^*(qp^*)^*.
p(qp)^* \equiv (pq)^*p.
(p+q^*)^* \equiv (p+q)^*.
If p\equiv q, then pr \equiv qr and rp \equiv rq.
If \mathscr{L}(q) \subseteq \mathscr{L}(p), then p^*q^* \equiv q^*p^* \equiv p^*.
p^* \equiv (\varepsilon+ p)^* \equiv (\varepsilon+ p)(p^*pp)^*.
p^*pp + \varepsilon\equiv (p^*pp)^* \equiv (pp+ppp)^*.
(🔥) p^*(q+rp^*)^* \equiv (p+q^*r)^*q^*.
(🔥) (qq+qp+p)^*qpp^* \equiv p^*q(pp^*q+qp^*q)^*pp^*.
(🔥) (\varepsilon+ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}})\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^*(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}} + \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{bba}}^*)^* \equiv \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^*(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}} + \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{bb}} + \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{bbb}})^*\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^*.







TipHint





To prove some of the items (especially, the last three), it is useful to apply previous equivalences.






Deciding whether two regular expressions are equivalent is \mathbf{PSPACE}-complete, i.e., informally, it is the hardest among the decision problems solvable using a polynomial amount of memory, but no limitations on the running time.

Exercise 12.4 Given a regular expression r and a word w, give an algorithm that with input r and w decides whether w\in \mathscr{L}(r) or not. What is the asymptotic cost of your algorithm w.r.t. the number of symbols in r and w?

A possibility is to use the Brzozowski derivative (see Chapter 6).

title: 12  Regular expressions
text:
12.2 From DFAs to regular expressions
In this section we show how to associate to a DFA an equivalent regular expression. That is, given a DFA A, using Arden’s lemma (Lemma 12.1 below), we show a way to construct a regular expression r s.t. \mathscr{L}(r)=\mathscr{L}(A).2

Lemma 12.1 (Arden’s Lemma) Given A,B\subseteq \Sigma^*, consider the equation 
X=A X\cup B\ ,
\tag{12.1} then X=A^* B is the smallest solution of Equation 12.1.
If \varepsilon\notin A then, this is the only solution. If \varepsilon\in A, then for every C\subseteq \Sigma^*, X=A^*(B\cup C) is a solution of Equation 12.1.






NoteProof





First we check that A^* B is always a solution of Equation 12.1: 
A(A^* B)\cup B = A^+ B\cup B = (A^+\cup \{\varepsilon\}) B = A^* B\ .
 If L is a solution of Equation 12.1, we show, by induction on n that L\supseteq A^nB. This implies immediately that L\supseteq A^*B.
Base case (n=0): L=AL\cup B, so in particular L\supseteq B=A^0B.
Inductive case: if L\supseteq A^nB, then L=AL\cup B\supseteq AA^nB=A^{n+1}B.
Hence X=A^*B is the smallest (w.r.t. inclusion) solution of Equation 12.1.
If \varepsilon\in A, then 
A(A^*(B\cup C))=A^+(B\cup C)\stackrel{\varepsilon\in A}{=}A^*(B\cup C)\ ,
 for every language C\subseteq \Sigma^*.
If \varepsilon\notin A, assume L is a solution of Equation 12.1 but, for sake of contradiction, L\neq A^*B. Since every solution must contain A^*B, it must be the case that L\not\subseteq A^*B. Let w be the shortest word in L but not in A^*B. Since L is a solution of Equation 12.1, then w\in AL\cup B. But clearly w\notin B (since B\subseteq A^*B and w\notin A^*B), hence w\in AL. This means w=w^\prime w^{\prime\prime} with w^\prime\in A and w^{\prime\prime}\in L. Since \varepsilon\notin A, then |w^\prime|>0 and |w^{\prime\prime}|<|w|.
We have now that w^{\prime\prime}\in L but w^{\prime\prime}\notin A^*B, otherwise w\in A^*B. This is a contradiction, since we assumed w to be the shortest word in L\setminus A^*B.









Dean N. Arden (1925-2018)


Using Arden’s Lemma we can then prove the following theorem.

Theorem 12.1 Given a DFA A, there exists a regular expression r s.t. \mathscr{L}(r)=\mathscr{L}(A).






NoteProof (sketch)





Let A=(Q,\Sigma,q_0,F,\delta) be a DFA. For each q\in Q, let X_q be the language of all words that would be accepted by A if q were the initial state (instead of q_0). Notice that 
X_q=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\bigcup_{\substack{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\in \Sigma\\\delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}})=q'}} \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\}X_{q'}&\text{ if } q\notin F\ ,
\\
\displaystyle
\{\varepsilon\}\cup \bigcup_{\substack{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\in \Sigma\\\delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}})=q'}} \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\}X_{q'} &\text{ if } q\in F\ .
\end{cases}
\tag{12.2}
This gives a system of equations where the variables are X_q and with Arden’s lemma (Lemma 12.1) we can find a way to express each X_q only using unions, concatenations, and Kleene stars, that is we have found a regular expression for it. This is analogous to the way to solve linear equations by eliminating variables. This analogy is even more clear if we write down Equation 12.2 using the notation for regular expressions: 
X_q=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\sum_{\substack{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\in \Sigma\\\delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}})=q'}} \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}X_{q'}&\text{ if } q\notin F\ ,
\\
\displaystyle
\varepsilon+ \sum_{\substack{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\in \Sigma\\\delta(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}})=q'}} \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}X_{q'} &\text{ if } q\in F\ .
\end{cases}
 Therefore, to find a regular expression for \mathscr{L}(A) we just need to solve the system above and the regular expression for X_{q_0} gives the answer. The fact that the system of equations always has a solution is left as an exercise (Exercise 12.5).





Exercise 12.5 Show that the system of equations Equation 12.2 in the proof of Theorem 12.1 has always a solution.






TipHint





Show that it is always possible to eliminate variables X_q one by one to get a system of equations with less and less variables X_q.





Example 12.2 Consider the language L=\{w\in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}^* :|w|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}}\in 2\mathbb N\}. The minimal DFA recognizing it is the following.






Figure 12.1



The system of equations associated to it is

\left\{
\begin{align*}
X_0 &= \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}X_0\cup \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}\}X_1\cup\{\varepsilon\}\\
X_1 &= \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}X_1\cup \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}\}X_0
\end{align*}
\right.
 Since in the end we are interested into giving a regular expression usually the system above is written directly as equations on regular expressions 
\left\{
\begin{align*}
X_0 &= \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}X_0+ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}X_1+\varepsilon\\
X_1 &= \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}X_1+ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}X_0
\end{align*}
\right.
 We can apply Arden’s Lemma to both equations, but since in the end we are interested into writing down a regular expression for X_0 let’s use the rule on the second equation:

X_1=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^*\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}X_0\ ,
 and substitute it into the first: 
\begin{align*}
X_0 &= \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}X_0+ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^*\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}X_0+\varepsilon
\\
& =(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}+\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^*\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}})X_0+\varepsilon\ .
\end{align*}
 Applying Arden’s Lemma again we get 
\begin{align*}
X_0 &= (\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}+\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^*\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}})^*\varepsilon
\\
&= (\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}+\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^*\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}})^*\ .
\end{align*}
 Hence we got a regular expression for L: (\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}+\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^*\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}})^*.

 (Use the DFA you constructed in Exercise 10.3.)

13.1 Closure properties
In this chapter we collect sistematically some results we saw in previous chapters (Chapter 9 and Chapter 12): make sure you have already read them!
We saw that there are three different ways to describe some languages:
In particular, we proved theorems that showed the equivalence of the three models. We collect such results in Theorem 13.1 below.
The previous theorem justifies the following definition.
In particular, to show that a language L is regular you don’t need to construct a DFA! You have the freedom of constructing a \varepsilon-NFA or a regular expression!
In the previous chapters we saw (or left as exercise to show) that \mathbf{Regular} is closed under union, intersection, complement, reverse, concatenation, Kleene star, homomorphisms, and inverse homomorphisms.
For each operation, the cost of computing the resulting language depends on how the input languages are presented (as regexes/DFAs/\varepsilon-NFAs) and how we want to present the output language.

title: 14  Non-regularity
text:
14.1 Non-regularity via fooling sets
In this chapter we see some techniques useful to show that a language is not in \mathbf{Regular}. One technique (the fooling sets, see Section 14.1) is also useful to show lower bounds on the number of states of the minimum DFA accepting a regular language.
The first technique we see is the use of fooling sets. This is useful to show that some given language L is not regular or that no DFA with few states can accept L.
Theorem 14.1 is actually an if and only if but we are only interested in the implication useful to prove limitations of DFAs.
We can use it to prove that a language is not in \mathbf{Regular} as in the following example.
We can also use Theorem 14.1 to show that some automata is actually the smallest possible, as in the next examples.
A less trivial example is the following.

title: 14  Non-regularity
text:
Definition 14.1 (fooling set) Given a language L\subseteq \Sigma^*, a set F\subseteq \Sigma^* is a fooling set for L if for every x,y\in F with x\neq y there exists z\in \Sigma^* s.t. xz\in L and yz\notin L.


Theorem 14.1 If F is a fooling set for L, then there is no DFA A with strictly less than |F| states s.t. L=\mathscr{L}(A). In particular, if F is infinite then L\notin \mathbf{Regular}.






NoteProof





Assume, towards a contradiction, that there exists a DFA A with strictly less than |F| states and such that L=\mathscr{L}(A). Let q_0 be the initial state of A and q_0w be the state of A in which we end-up when reading the word w.
By the pigeonhole principle (see Chapter 2), there are exist x,y\in F with x\neq y s.t. q_0x=q_0y. Since F is a fooling set, exists z\in\Sigma^* s.t. xz\in L and yz\notin L. That is q_0xz is a final state and q_0yz is not a final state. Since q_0x=q_0y then q_0xz=q_0yz, and this gives the desired contradiction.







Example 14.1 L=\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n :n\in \mathbb{N}\}\notin \mathbf{Regular}.
By Theorem 14.1, it is enough to construct an infinite fooling set for L. Consider F=\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n :n\in \mathbb{N}\}. Given two distinct words x,y\in F we must have x=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n and y=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^m with n\neq m. We can then choose z=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n. We have that xz=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n\in L and yz=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^m\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n\notin L (since n\neq m). That is F is a fooling set for L.



Example 14.2 As a first example we show that the minimum DFA for the language 
L=\{w \in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}^* :\mathtt{value}_2(w)\in 3\mathbb N\}
 has at least 3 states. (Did you construct a minimal DFA for this language in Exercise 10.3?)
Consider the set F=\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{10}}\}. We show that F is a fooling set. Let’s consider the different possibilities for x\neq y in F and for each of them a possible z to choose s.t. xz\in L and yz\notin L:

Example 14.3 Given n\in \mathbb N, consider the language 
L_n=\{x\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}y :x,y\in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}^* \land |y|=n\}\ .
 In Exercise 9.11, you constructed a DFA B with 2^{n+1} states s.t. \mathscr{L}(B)=L_n. We construct now a fooling set F for L_n of size 2^{n+1}. This, thanks to Theorem 14.1 implies that B must be minimal. Another consequence is that the DFA B obtained in Theorem 9.2, in the worst case, might be exponentially larger than the corresponding NFA A.
Take F=\{w\in\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}^* :|w|=n+1\}. The set F clearly has the correct size, and we prove now it is a fooling set for L_n. Given distinct x,y\in F, let i the largest index s.t. x[i]\neq y[i]. W.l.o.g. let x[i]=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}} and y[i]=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}. If i=1 (recall that we start numbering the positions in a word from 1), take z=\varepsilon, if i=2 take z=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}, and in general take z=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^{i-1}. We have that xz has an \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}} in position n+1 from the end, while yz has a \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}} in position n+1 from the end. That is xz\in L_n while yz\notin L_n. This concludes the proof that F is a fooling set for L_n.






Notice that i being the largest index s.t. x[i]\neq y[i] is not important: any index i s.t. x[i]\neq y[i] would work as-well. And similarly z=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^{i-1} is also not-important: any word z of length i-1 would also work.





Exercise 14.1 To make sure you understood the argument in Example 14.3, prove that F=\{w\in\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}^* :|w|=n+2\} is not a fooling set for L_n by showing it does not match the definition of fooling set.

\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^{F_n} :n\in \mathbb{N}\}, where F_n is the nth Fibonacci number.
(🔥) \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^{p_n} :n\in \mathbb{N}\}, where p_n is the nth prime number.
(🔥) \{w\in \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}^* :\exists n\in \mathbb{N}\ \mathsf{value}_{2}(w)=n^2\}, where \mathsf{value}_{2}(w) is the natural number whose binary representation is w.

title: 14  Non-regularity
text:
14.2 Non-regularity via closure properties
Closure properties can be used to show that a language L is not in \mathbf{Regular}, by reducing this to the known fact that another (usually simpler) language L' is not in \mathbf{Regular}. This is essentially using the contrapositive of the closure properties.

Example 14.4 For example, \mathbf{Regular} being closed intersection means that if L_1 and L_2 are in \mathbf{Regular} then L_1\cap L_2 is in \mathbf{Regular} too. Which, taking the contrapositive, can be equivalently stated as:
If L_1\cap L_2\notin \mathbf{Regular} then either L_2\notin \mathbf{Regular} or L_2\notin\mathbf{Regular}.
This immediately gives that \{w\in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}^* :|w|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}}=|w|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}}\}\notin \mathbf{Regular}.






TipHow?






\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n :n\in \mathbb{N}\}=\{w\in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}^* :|w|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}}=|w|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}}\}\cap \mathscr{L}(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^*\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^*)\ .
 Since \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n :n\in \mathbb{N}\}\notin\mathbf{Regular} (as we saw in Example 14.1), then either \{w\in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}^* :|w|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}}=|w|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}}\}\notin\mathbf{Regular} or \mathscr{L}(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^*\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^*)\notin\mathbf{Regular}. But clearly \mathscr{L}(\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^*\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^*)\in \mathbf{Regular}, therefore \{w\in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}^* :|w|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}}=|w|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}}\}\notin\mathbf{Regular}.










Caution



If you are not absolutely sure of what you are doing, always use closure properties in the forward direction. That is, establish that L and L' are regular, then conclude that L \circ L' must be regular (for some operation \circ).



Exercise 14.3 Only using that \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n :n\in \mathbb{N}\}\notin\mathbf{Regular} and the closure properties of \mathbf{Regular} show that the following languages are also not in \mathbf{Regular}:

(🌱) \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^n :n\in \mathbb{N}\}

\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{c}}^n :n\in \mathbb{N}\}
\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^{2n}\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n :n\in \mathbb{N}\}
\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^m :\text{if }n \text{ is odd then } n=m\}
\{w\in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}^* :\exists n\in \mathbb{N}\text{ s.t. }\mathsf{value}_{2}(w)=2^n(2^n-1)\}
(🔥) C++ (the programming language)






TipHint





Focus on very simple C++ programs with the same number of open { and }.






TipMore hint





The programs of the form int main (){}, int main (){{}}, int main (){{{}}}, …









Exercise 14.4 (🔥🔥) Can we prove using only \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n :n\in \mathbb{N}\}\notin\mathbf{Regular} and the closure properties of \mathbf{Regular} that every non-regular language L\subseteq \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}^* is indeed non-regular?






TipHint





Compare the cardinality of the non-regular languages L\subseteq \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}^* vs the cardinality of the languages that you can describe using closure properties of \mathbf{Regular}, languages in \mathbf{Regular} and \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n :n\in \mathbb{N}\}.

title: 14  Non-regularity
text:
14.3 Non-regularity via Pumping Lemma
Another way to prove that a given language is non-regular is the Pumping Lemma. Theorem 14.1 relied on the pigeonhole principle to show that a language is non-regular. The Pumping Lemma below also relies on the pigeonhole principle but used in a different way.

Lemma 14.1 (Pumping Lemma for regular languages) Let L\subseteq \Sigma^*. If for every p\in \mathbb{N}, there exist a word w\in\Sigma^* s.t.

|w|\geqslant p,
w\in L, and
for every x,y,z\in \Sigma^* s.t. w=xyz, y\neq \varepsilon and |xy|\leqslant p there exist k\in \mathbb{N} s.t. xy^kz\notin L,

then L\notin\mathbf{Regular}.






NoteProof





Suppose, towards a contradiction, that L\in \mathbf{Regular}. Then by Definition 13.1 and Theorem 13.1, there must exist a DFA A=(Q,\Sigma,\{q_0\},F,\delta) s.t. \mathscr{L}(A)=L.
We want to show that the hypothesis of the lemma must be false, that is we want to show that

there exists a p\in \mathbb N s.t. for every word w\in\Sigma^*, if |w|\geqslant p and w\in L, then there exist x,y,z\in \Sigma^* s.t. w=xyz, y\neq \varepsilon, |xy|\leqslant p and for every k\in \mathbb{N} xy^kz\in L.

Let p=|Q| and w be an arbitrary word s.t. w\in L and |w|=n\geqslant p. Let w[i] be the i-th symbol of w (we start counting from 1) and w[i:j] (with i\leqslant j) be the concatenation of the symbols of w between positions i and j included.
Since w\in L, there must exist a sequence of states q_0,q_1,\dots,q_n\in Q s.t. q_n\in F and for each i\in \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}, \delta(q_i,w[i])=q_{i+1}. The tuple of states q_0,\dots,q_n has size n+1>p=|Q|, hence by the pigeonhole principle (see Section 2.2.1), the states q_0,\dots,q_n cannot be all distinct. Let \ell be the first index in the sequence s.t. exists i<\ell with q_i=q_\ell.
Let x=w[1:i] (if i=0 take x=\varepsilon), y=w[i+1:\ell], and z=w[\ell+1:n]. See Figure 21.1 for a visual depiction of the paths giving x,y,z.






Figure 14.1



The states from q_0,\dots,q_{\ell-1} must be all distinct, by the choice of \ell. Hence \ell\leqslant|Q|=p and |xy|=\ell\leqslant p. It is also immediate to see that y\neq \varepsilon.
To conclude we need to show that for every k\in \mathbb N, xy^k z\in L. It is immediate to construct a path accepting the word xy^kz: take the original path but repeat the cycle between the q_i and q_\ell k-times.




The Pumping Lemma is essentially saying that we can win the following game. Given a language L we want to prove is not regular:

the “adversary” picks p\in \mathbb N (p is usually called the pumping length);
we choose a word w\in L with |w|\geqslant p (as a function of p);
the adversary chooses x,y,z s.t.

w=xyz
|xy|\leqslant p
y\neq \varepsilon

we choose k\in \mathbb N (as a function of n,x,y,z)
if we prove that xy^kz\notin L we win (i.e. we proved L is not a regular language).

Hence a “template” for a proof using the pumping lemma for regular languages is as follow:

We prove that L is non-regular using the pumping lemma. Let p be the pumping length. Consider the word w=..... We have that |w|\geqslant p and w\in L (this needs an argument, possibly trivial, but you need to check it). Given an arbitrary decomposition of w as w=xyz, with |xy|\leqslant p and y\neq \varepsilon, consider the natural number k=..... To conclude we need to prove that xy^kz\notin L (this needs an argument, usually quite non-trivial).


Example 14.5 Following the template, above we show (again) that 
L=\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n :n\in \mathbb N\}\notin \mathbf{Regular}\ .
 We already saw a proof of this fact in Example 14.1 using a fooling set.
We prove that L is non-regular using the pumping lemma. Let p be the pumping length. Consider the word w=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^p\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^p. We have that |w|\geqslant p and clearly w\in L. Given an arbitrary decomposition of w as w=xyz, with |xy|\leqslant p and y\neq \varepsilon, consider the natural number k=0. To conclude we need to prove that xy^kz\notin L. Since |xy|\leqslant p it must be that x=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^i, y=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^j and z=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^{p-i-j}\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^p. Since y\neq \varepsilon, then j> 0. The word xy^kz=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^{p+j(k-1)}\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^p=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^{p-j}\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^p. Since j>0, then p-j\neq p and xy^0z\notin L.







WarningCommon errors



To avoid errors in the use of the Pumping Lemma stick to the proof template. The creative part is in the choice of the orange parts not in the structure of the argument.

We cannot use the Pumping Lemma to show that a language L\in \mathbf{Regular}. The Pumping Lemma is not an if and only if.
The word w must depend on p. If our choice of w does not depend on p then it is wrong.
The word w cannot depend on x,y,z. If our choice of w does depend on x,y,z then it is wrong.
The word w does not need to have length exactly p, it might be much much larger, for example p!.
Another common error is to choose x,y,z. We cannot choose them! The only things we know about them is that w=xyz, |xy|\leqslant p and y\neq\varepsilon. The adversary chooses x,y,z with the given constraints, not us.
Another common error is to assume x\neq\varepsilon! It might be that x=\varepsilon, the part we know it is non-empty is y!
Choosing k=1 will never work. Often k=0 is a good choice but not always. Remember that k doesn’t need to be a fixed constant, it might depend on p and x,y,z.




Exercise 14.5 Prove again that the languages in Exercise 14.3 are non-regular but now using the Pumping Lemma (and possibly some closure property of regular languages).

title: Context-Free Languages
text:
Goals
In this part of the course we focus on studying context-free languages, which are languages generated by context-free grammars or accepted by pushdown automata.
Context-free languages are more powerful than regular languages and are widely used in programming language design and implementation, as well as in natural language processing.
At the end of this part of the course you should be able to:

text:
16.1 \mathbf{Regular}\subsetneq \mathbf{CFL}
In this chapter we introduce context-free grammars and the class of languages they generate, the context-free languages. We also introduce some important properties of context-free languages, such as closure properties and normal forms.
Usually production rules on the same variable are grouped together and we write A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha_1\ \vert\ \alpha_2\ \vert\ \ldots\ \vert\ \alpha_k instead of writing k rules A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha_1,\dots,A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha_k.
To define the language generated by a context-free grammar we first need to define the derivation relation. Given a context-free grammar G=(V,\Sigma,R,S), the derivation relation \Rightarrow is a binary relation on (V\cup \Sigma)^* defined as follows: for any u,v\in (V\cup \Sigma)^*, A\in V, and \alpha\in (V\cup \Sigma)^*, we have uAv\Rightarrow u\alpha v if A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha\in R. If w_0,w_1,\dots,w_n\in (V\cup \Sigma)^* are such that w_i\Rightarrow w_{i+1} for all i=0,1,\dots,n-1, then we write w_0\Rightarrow^* w_n and we say that w_n is derivable from w_0. The number n is the number of steps of the derivation.
Let’s see a couple of examples. In the first one (Example 16.3) we are given a context-free grammar and we want to find the language it generates. In the second one (Example 16.4) we are given a language and we want to find a context-free grammar that generates it.
Notice that in both examples we had a claim of the form \mathscr{L}(G)=L and we proved it by proving the two containments \mathscr{L}(G)\subseteq L and \mathscr{L}(G)\supseteq L. This is a common technique to prove that a context-free grammar generates a given language.
The containment \mathscr{L}(G)\subseteq L is usually proved by induction on the number of derivation steps. To make the induction work it is often needed to transform the grammar G into an equivalent one G' that is in a certain normal form, for example to ensure that at each derivation step the length of the words strictly increses (see Section 18.1).
The containment \mathscr{L}(G)\supseteq L is usually proved by induction on the length of the words in L (or some related parameter).
So far we have seen grammars that only have one variable. Let’s see some simple example with more than one variable.
In this section we prove that every regular language is also a context-free language and if the alphabet has size at least 2 then there is a language that is context-free but not regular. We do this via guided exercises that incidentally use closure properties of context-free languages to prove the result.
Now, is \mathbf{Regular}\neq \mathbf{CFL}?
In general yes, they are different but not always. It depends on the alphabet size. In fact, if |\Sigma|=1, then \mathbf{Regular}= \mathbf{CFL}. However, if \Sigma=\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\}, then \mathbf{Regular}\subsetneq \mathbf{CFL}. In fact, the language \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n : n\in \mathbb{N}\} is context-free but not regular (see Example 14.1 and Example 16.4).
The fact that if |\Sigma|=1, then \mathbf{Regular}= \mathbf{CFL} is not obvious and it is a consequence of Parikh’s theorem. We will not prove this theorem in this course. The fact that for |\Sigma|=1 some classes of languages coincide is the reason why in The Big Picture Figure 1 we decided to show inclusions between classes of languages for a binary alphabet.
The proof that \mathbf{Regular}\subseteq \mathbf{CFL} from Exercise 16.3 does not give a direct way to construct a context-free grammar G for a given regular language L when L is presented giving a DFA. In the next exercise we show how to do this.

title: 16  Context-Free Grammars
text:
16.3 Well-balanced parentheses
We conclude this chapter with a notable language in \mathbf{CFL}: the language of well-balanced parentheses. This a prototypical example of context-free language: the language of words that are well-balanced parentheses.

Definition 16.3 (Well-balanced parentheses) The language of well-balanced parentheses is the language \mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}1\subseteq\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{(}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)}}\}^* with the following properties: \mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}1 is the smallest (w.r.t. inclusion) language L\subseteq\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{(}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)}}\}^* s.t.

\varepsilon\in L;
if x,y\in L then xy\in L;
if x\in L, then \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{(}}x\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)}}\in L.


From this recursive definition it is immediate to get a context-free grammar G generating \mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}1:

\begin{array}{lcl}
S\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ SS\ \vert\ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{(}}S\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)}}\ \vert\ \varepsilon\ .
\end{array}
\tag{16.1}

Exercise 16.7 Show that \mathscr{L}(G)=\mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}1, where G is the grammar in Equation 16.1.






Walther von Dyck (1856-1934)



Exercise 16.8 Show that

\mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}1=\{w\in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{(}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)}}\}^* :|w|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{(}}}=|w|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)}}}\land \forall x,y (w=xy\implies |x|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{(}}}\geqslant|x|_{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{)}}})\}\ ,
 that is w\in \mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}1 if and only if it has the same number of open and closed parentheses and in every prefix of w, the number of open parentheses is always greater than or equal to the number of closed parentheses.


Exercise 16.9 Generalize the construction in Definition 16.3 to get \mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}s, that is the language of well-balanced parentheses but now instead of having only 1 type of parentheses we have s types of parentheses. For example, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{[([]())]()}}\in \mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}2 but \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{([)]}}\notin\mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}2. Construct a grammar for \mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}2 and in general for \mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}s.

The language \mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}s is important because it is the most difficult context-free language, in the following sense.

Theorem 16.1 (Chomsky–Schützenberger representation theorem) A language L\subseteq \Sigma^* is in \mathbf{CFL} if and only if

L=\sigma(\mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}s\cap R)\ ,
 where s\geqslant 1, R is a regular language (over the alphabet of \mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}s \Gamma_s), and \sigma is a homomorphism from \Gamma_s to \Sigma^*.






Noam Chomsky (1928-)





Marcel-Paul Schützenberger(1920-1996)


Although this result characterizes \mathbf{CFL}, to show that a language L\in \mathbf{CFL} it is easier to just construct a context-free grammar generating L and to show that L\notin\mathbf{CFL} we will use the Pumping Lemma (see Chapter 21). We mention this result here just to highlight the importance of the \mathsf{Dyck}\text{-}s languages.

title: 17  Parsing and Ambiguity
text:
17.1 The CYK algorithm
In this chapter we expand on the concept of parsing and ambiguity. They come into play since one important use of context-free grammars is to specify all the valid programs of a given programming language.
Now, to each derivation of w we can associate a parse tree (using the rules of the derivation) and viceversa, a parse tree may correspond to several possible derivations of w, depending on the order in which the non-terminals are expanded.
If the non-terminal variables describe operations, then we can use a parse tree to associate a priority among the operations and hence an intended meaning of the word w.
A common way to check that two parse trees for a word w are non-isomorphic is to do a pre-order (Root, Left, Right) traversal on both of them. This corresponds to the so called leftmost derivation of w: at each step of the derivation of w the non-terminal to expand is the leftmost in the string. Two leftmost derivations are distinct if at some step either they expand a different non-terminal or they expand the same non-terminal but with a different rule. Using a post-order traversal gives the notion of rightmost derivation.
Sometimes it is possible to remove the ambibuity from a grammar giving another grammar generating the same language but now unambiguous. Other times it is not possible, there are languages in \mathbf{CFL} where every possible grammar generating them is ambiguous (they are called inherently ambiguous context-free languages).
Given a grammar G=(V,\Sigma, R,S) and a word w a natural problem is to decide whether w\in \mathscr{L}(G) and if this is the case to construct a parse tree for w. In this section, we describe an algorithm to solve this problem: the Cocke–Younger–Kasami (CYK) parsing algorithm. This is an example of the common technique of dynamic programming.
As we see in Chapter 18 this is not an unreasonable assumption since every context-free grammar can be transformed into an equivalent one of this form and the new grammar has size at most |G|^2, where |G| denotes the size of the grammar (for example, the total length of its productions).
By the special form of the grammar, if w=\varepsilon it is trivial to check whether w\in \mathscr{L}(G). So we can also assume w\neq \varepsilon. Let n=|w|.
The idea of the algorithm is not only to decide whether w\in \mathscr{L}(G), but for each subword of w to know what variables can generate it. To store this information we can use Boolean variables P[i,\ell,A], for 1\leqslant i\leqslant n, 1\leqslant\ell\leqslant n-i+1 and A\in V, with intended meaning the truth value of “the subword of w starting in position i and of length \ell can be generated from the variable A”. (As usual, we use the convention that w[1] is the first symbol of w, that is w=w[1]w[2]\cdots w[n].)
Our goal is to compute the truth value of P[1,n,S] since P[1,n,S]=1 if and only if w\in \mathscr{L}(G) by construction.
It is immediate to know the values of P[i,1,A] for each i\leqslant n and A\in V. How?
Now, in a typical dynamic programming approach, you want to compute all truth values P[i,\ell,A] assuming you already know all the truth values P[i,k,A] with k<\ell. How
Following this approach, a possible pseudocode implementing the CYK algorithm is the following.
The cost of the previous algorithm is \mathcal{O}(n^3|G|).
A natural question to ask is whether the CYK algorithm we described has the optimal running time \mathcal{O}(n^3|G|) for deciding whether w\in \mathscr{L}(G). This is not the case and (surprisingly) parsing for context-free grammars is tightly connected with matrix multiplication of 0/1-valued matrices.
On one side Valiant (1975) showed that algorithms for fast multiplication of 0/1-valued matrices can be used to do the computations in the CYK algorithm. On the other side Lee (2002) showed that any parsing algorithm for CFGs with running time \mathcal{O}(n^{3-\varepsilon}|G|) can be turned into an algorithm to compute the product of n\times n 0/1-valued matrices in time \mathcal{O}(n^{3-\varepsilon/3}).

title: 17  Parsing and Ambiguity
text:
John Cocke (1925-2002)








Important



A reference for the CYK algorithm is (Kozen 1997, chap. 27).








TipAssumption on the form of G



For simplicity, we assume all the productions of G have the form A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ BC with A,B,C\in V or A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}} with \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\in \Sigma (or S\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \varepsilon if \varepsilon\in \mathscr{L}(G)).




Exercise 17.7 Show that for a grammar G of the form above any production of a non-empty word of length n consists of the application of exactly 2n-1 productions.











NoteAnswer





P[i,1,A]=1 if and only if A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ w[i] is a production rule of G. Notice that here we are using crucially the assumption on the special form of the grammar G.










NoteAnswer





For a fixed i with 1\leqslant i\leqslant n, P[i,\ell,A]=1 if and only if exists 1\leqslant k\leqslant\ell-1 and a production A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ BC, where both P[i,k,B] and P[i+k,\ell-k,C] are both true.




Exercise 17.8 Using the CYK algorithm as described above, decide whether w=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{aabbab}} is in \mathscr{L}(G) where G is the following grammar

\begin{array}{lcl}
S\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ AB\ \vert\  BA \ \vert\ SS\ \vert\ AC\ \vert\ BD\\
C\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ SB\\
D\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ SA\\
A\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}\\
B\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}
\end{array}





\begin{algorithm} \caption{CYK Algorithm}\begin{algorithmic} \Input{A non-empty word $w = w[1] \cdots w[n]$ and a grammar $G=(V,\Sigma,R,S)$ meeting the assumptions above} \Output{The answer to the question: $w\in \mathscr{L}(G)$?} \State{Initialize all $P[i,\ell,A]$ to $0$} \For{$i = 1$ to $n$} \Comment{Initialization: setting all $P[i,1,A]$s} \ForAll{$A \in V$} \If{$(A \to w[i]) \in R$} \State $P[i,1,A] = 1$ \EndIf \EndFor \EndFor \For{$\ell = 2$ to $n$} \Comment{Fill the table in increasing order of substring length} \For{$i = 1$ to $n-\ell+1$} \For{$k = 1$ to $\ell-1$} \ForAll{$(A \to BC) \in R$} \If{$P[i,k,B] \land P[i+k,\ell-k,C]$} \State $P[i,\ell,A] = 1$ \EndIf \EndFor \EndFor \EndFor \EndFor \State \Return $P[1,n,S]$ \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}




Exercise 17.9 Try to adapt the CYK algorithm to a general grammar. What problems might occur? How does the running time change?


Exercise 17.10 Adapt the previous code to also obtain a parse tree of w when w\in \mathscr{L}(G).


Exercise 17.11 Adapt the previous code to also know whether G generates w ambiguously or not, i.e. whether there are at least two distinct parse trees for w.

Lee, Lillian. 2002. “Fast Context-Free Grammar Parsing Requires Fast Boolean Matrix Multiplication.” Journal of the ACM 49 (1): 1–15. https://doi.org/10.1145/505241.505242.


Valiant, Leslie G. 1975. “General Context-Free Recognition in Less Than Cubic Time.” Journal of Computer and System Sciences 10 (2): 308–15. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-0000(75)80046-8.

title: 18  Chomsky Normal Form and CFG depuration
text:
18.1 Depuration of Grammars
In this chapter we introduce some transformations on grammars that could be used as a prepocessing step of some algorithms (e.g. the CYK algorithm Section 17.1) or could simplify inductive arguments.
Given a context-free grammar G=(V,\Sigma,P,S), the term depuration refers to the process of constructing an equivalent grammar G' more structured and without clearly redundant variables.
The transformations above might interfere with each other un-doing the work of previous transformations.

title: 18  Chomsky Normal Form and CFG depuration
text:
Important



A reference for this part of the course is (Hopcroft et al. 2007, sec. 7.1).



Removing useless variablesRemoving all A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \varepsilonRemoving all A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ B


A variable of G is useful if it is involved in a production of a string of only terminal symbols, that is a variable is useful if it is reachable from S and it is productive.
We can define the reachable variables recursively follows: S is reachable from S (clearly), and if A is reachable and we have a rule A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha with \alpha\in (V\cup \Sigma)^* then all the variables in \alpha are also reachable. Once we identified the reachable variables R\subseteq V, we can then remove all the the productions B\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \beta with B\notin R.
We can define productive variables as the ones that eventually are able to generate a word in \Sigma^*. This can be computed using a recursive approach: if A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha and \alpha\in \Sigma^*, then A is productive; if A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha with \alpha\in (V\cup \Sigma)^* and every variable in \alpha is productive, then A is productive. Once we identified the productive variables R\subseteq V, we can then remove all the the productions B\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \beta with B\notin R or with some variable in \beta not in R.






Warning



The order in which we perform the operations matters. Consider the grammar 
\begin{array}{lcl}
S\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ AB\ \vert\  \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}\\
B\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}
\end{array}
 if we remove unreachable variables first and then the unproductive variables we still get a grammar with useless symbols. You need to remove the unproductive variables first, and then the unreachable ones.




A production of the form A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \varepsilon is a \varepsilon-production.
A variable A is nullable if it can derive the empty word \varepsilon. We can define recursively nullable variables: if A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \varepsilon is a production, then A is nullable; if A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha and \alpha\in V^* with all the variables in \alpha nullable then A is also nullable.
Once we identified the nullable variables, we can then remove all productions of the form A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \varepsilon (with A\neq S), and for every production A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha B\beta with B nullable, add the production A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\  \alpha\beta, and keep symplifying the new set of productions. Unless A=S, never write productions A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \varepsilon that might occur.

Example 18.1 For example removing the \varepsilon-productions from the grammar 
\begin{array}{lcl}
S\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ ABC\ \vert\ \varepsilon\\
A\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ \varepsilon\\
B\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ \varepsilon\\
C\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ \varepsilon
\end{array}
 gives the grammar S\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ ABC\ \vert\ AB\ \vert\ AC\ \vert\ BC\ \vert\ A \ \vert\ B\ \vert\ C\ \vert\ \varepsilon. Where clearly the variables A,B,C are useless.



A production of the form A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ B is called unit production. The variable A is clearly redundant, its only job is to get expanded into B. Productions of the form A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ B where a is a terminal are not unit productions. The technique to remove all unit productions that simply expands them until they disappear often works but not always. Consider for instance the productions A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ B, B\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ C, C\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ A. What works is the following:

find all unit pairs, i.e. pairs of variables (A,B) where B can be derived from A using only unit productions. As for the other cases, there is an inductive construction of unit pairs: for each variable A, (A,A) is a unit pair; and if (A,B) is a unit pair and B\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ C is a production, the (A,C) is also a unit pair.
for each unit pair (A,B) add all the productions A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha to G', where B\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha is a nonunit production in \mathcal P. For the unit pair (A,A) we add as productions in G' all nonunit productions of A.


Example 18.2 For example, removing the unit rules from the grammar 
\begin{array}{lcl}
S\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ X_1\\
X_1\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ X_2\\
\vdots &\\
X_{n-1}\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ X_n\\
X_n\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ w
\end{array}
 with w\in \Sigma^*, gives the grammar

\begin{array}{lcl}
S\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ w\\
X_1\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ w\\
\vdots &\\
X_{n-1}\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ w\\
X_n\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ w
\end{array}







Exercise 18.1 Find an order in which to apply the removal of useless variables, \varepsilon-productions, and unit productions to obtain an equivalent grammar.

title: 18  Chomsky Normal Form and CFG depuration
text:
18.2 Chomsky Normal Form
We conclude this chapter with a normal form for context-free grammars: the Chomsky Normal Form. This will be useful in some theoretical concstructions such as Example 21.1 or the Pumping Lemma (Lemma 21.1).

Definition 18.1 A grammar G=(V,\Sigma,R,S) is in Chomsky Normal Form if all its rules have one of the following forms

S\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \varepsilon, or
A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}} with \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\in \Sigma, or
A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ BC, with B,C\in V but B,C\neq S.



Theorem 18.1 Given a context-free grammar G, there is another context free grammar G' in Chomsky Normal Form s.t. \mathscr{L}(G)=\mathscr{L}(G').






NoteProof (sketch)





Transforming a grammar G into an equivalent one in Chomsky Normal Form is an algorithmic procedure:

Step 1: Create a new start symbol. Just have a new start symbol S' and add the production S'\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ S.
Step 2: Change nonsolitary terminals into variables. Change each rule of the form A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\beta into A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha N_s \beta and N_s\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}. Do this to all the rules removing terminals from RHS of the rules (unless it is the only symbol).
Step3: Make RHS at most binary. Transform each rule of the form A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ X_1X_2\cdots X_n with n\geqslant 3 into 
\begin{array}{lcl}
A\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ X_1A_1\\
A_1\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ X_2A_2\\
\vdots&&\\
A_{n-3}\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ X_{n-2}A_{n-2}\\
A_{n-2}\ &\boldsymbol{\to}&\ X_{n-1}X_n
\end{array}

Step 4: Eliminate all \varepsilon-productions. As we saw in Section 18.1.
Step 5: Eliminate unit productions. As we saw in Section 18.1.






Exercise 18.2 Show that the grammar constructed in the proof of Theorem 18.1 is indeed in Chomsky Normal Form and equivalent to G.


Exercise 18.3 Given a context-free grammar G, how many symbols could have the equivalent context-free grammar in Chomsky Normal Form obtained using the algorithm from the proof of Theorem 18.1 (w.r.t. the number of symbols in G)? What if you exchange the order of steps 3 and 4? Is the algorithm still correct? What is the cost now?





Hopcroft, John E., Rajeev Motwani, and Jeffrey D. Ullman. 2007. Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation. 3rd edition. Pearson Addison Wesley.

title: 19  Pushdown Automata
text:
19.1 PDAs and CFGs are equivalent models
In this chapter we show an equivalent way to describe the class of context-free languages (via the pushdown automata), we show that they are equivalent to context-free grammars, we show some further closure properties of context-free languages. This characterization of context-free languages via pushdown automata allows to define a natural special case of them which are the deterministic context-free languages.
A pushdown automaton is an \varepsilon-NFA (see Chapter 9) which is also allowed access to an external working memory in the form of a stack.
Transitions have the following form
which means:
Similarly,

The alphabet of the words we feed to the PDA and the stack are usually different. The convention is to use upper-case letters to denote the stack alphabet.
We also want to know when the stack is empty, to do so the convention is to have a symbol (usually denoted as \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{Z}}) to mark the bottom of the stack. We never want to pop \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{Z}}, that is, in transitions such as the ones of Figure 19.1 or Figure 19.2, if \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{T}} is \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{Z}}, then \alpha should start with \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{Z}}.
The formal definition of a pushdown automata is the following.
Given a PDA A, to describe how to use it to accept words in \Sigma^* we need the notion of instantaneous description, which informally is the current state the machine is in. It is a triple (q,x,\alpha)\in Q\times \Sigma^*\times \Gamma^* and the meaning is that
When reading w, the instantaneous description at the beginning is (q_0,w,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{Z}}), meaning that we are in the initial state of the PDA A, we still have to read the whole w, and the stack is empty (only \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{Z}}, the symbol marking the bottom of the stack, is in it).
Following a transition as the one in Figure 19.1 we go from the instantaneous description (q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}y,\beta\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{T}}) to the instantaneous description (q^\prime,y,\beta\alpha). We denote this with the notation 
(q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}y,\beta\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{T}}) \vdash_A (q^\prime,y,\beta\alpha)\ .
Similarly, following a transition as the one in Figure 19.2 we go from the instantaneous description (q,y,\beta\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{T}}) to the instantaneous description (q^\prime,y,\beta\alpha). We denote this with the notation 
(q,y,\beta\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{T}}) \vdash_A (q^\prime,y,\beta\alpha)\ .
In this section we show that contxt-free grammars and pushdown automata have the same expressive power. In the sense of Theorem 19.1 and Theorem 19.2 below.

title: 19  Pushdown Automata
text:
Theorem 19.1 Let L\subseteq \Sigma^*. If there is a CFG G s.t. \mathscr{L}(G)=L, then there is a PDA A s.t. \mathscr{L}(A)=L.






NoteProof (sketch)





Let G = (V, \Sigma, R, S) be a context-free grammar such that L = \mathscr{L}(G), where V is the set of variables, \Sigma is the terminal alphabet, R is the set of production rules, and S is the start variable.
A nondeterministic pushdown automaton B that simulates derivations in G has the following shape:






Figure 19.4



The transition \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\to \varepsilon is not a single one, there is one of them for each \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\in \Sigma. Similarly, also the transition \varepsilon,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{A}}\to \alpha^R is not a single one, there is one of them for each production rule A\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \alpha in the grammar G. The reason we have \varepsilon,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{A}}\to \alpha^R and not \varepsilon,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{A}}\to \alpha is the convention we used on how the words are put in the stack. If \alpha is in the stack, we chose to have the last symbol of \alpha as the top.
Intuitively, the construction is correct due to the following two observations. If w \in \mathscr{L}(G), then there is a derivation S \Rightarrow^* w. The PDA B can choose the corresponding production rules and match each terminal against the input, so it accepts w.
Conversely, every accepting computation of the PDA corresponds to a valid derivation of the input string from S. Therefore, the PDA accepts only strings in \mathscr{L}(G).
For a formal proof of the correctness of the construction see (Sipser 2013, sec. 2.2).





Exercise 19.4 Using the construction in the proof of Theorem 19.1 give a PDA accepting the same language as the grammar S\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}S\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}\ \vert\ \varepsilon.


Theorem 19.2 Let L\subseteq \Sigma^*. If there is a PDA A s.t. \mathscr{L}(A)=L, then there is a context-free grammar G s.t. \mathscr{L}(G)=L.






NoteProof (sketch)





Let the PDA A=(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,\delta,q_0,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{Z}},F). In this proof sketch we only give the context-free grammar G s.t. \mathscr{L}(G)=\mathscr{L}(A) and a proof sketch of why it is correct. For the full argument see (Sipser 2013, sec. 2.2).
To make the construction easier we first transform the PDA so that it has the following properties:

there is exactly one accepting state q_{accept};
the PDA empties the stack before accepting (we use the symbol \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{Z}} to denoe the bottom of an empty stack);
each transition is either a pop of exactly one symbol or a push of exactly one symbol.

The grammar G is based on the following idea:

For every pair of states q,q' of A, we have a variable S_{qq'} that generates the words that, in A, from state q and empty stack lead to q' with empty stack.

By the assumption 1, the initial variable of G is S_{q_0q_{accept}}. By assumptions 2 and 3, then the first operation on the stack is a push and the last one is a pop.
Now, for each q\in Q, \varepsilon leads from q (with empty stack) to q (with empty stack) so to the productions of G we add 
S_{qq}\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \varepsilon\ .

For each q,q'\in Q, it might be that the stack becomes empty in some intermediate state r\in Q, so, to the productions of G we add

S_{qq'}\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ S_{qr}S_{rq'}\ ,
 for each q,q,r\in Q.
The remaining productions deal with the case when the stack is empty only at the beginning and end. That is, for every q,q',p,p'\in Q, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{t}}\in \Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{U}}\in \Gamma, if (q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{Z}},p,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{ZU}})\in \delta and (p',\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{t}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{U}},q',\varepsilon)\in \delta, we have the production 
S_{qq'}\ \boldsymbol{\to}\ \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}S_{pp'}\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{t}}\ .
 That is, if the PDA accepts a word w=\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}w'\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{t}} and the stack is empty only at the edn, then it must go to a state p, push something (\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{U}}) in the stack, and only pops it at the end when reading \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{t}} from some state p'.





Exercise 19.5 Using the construction in the proof of Theorem 19.2 give a CFG accepting the same language as the PDA in Figure 19.3.

title: 19  Pushdown Automata
text:
19.2 Closure properties
In this section we conclude the closure properties of context-free languages (see Table 16.1).

Theorem 19.3 The intersection of a context-free language with a regular language is context-free, that is if L\in \mathbf{CFL} and L'\in \mathbf{Regular}, then L\cap L'\in \mathbf{CFL}.






NoteProof (sketch)





By Theorem 19.1, we have a PDA A s.t. \mathscr{L}(A)=L. Since L'\in \mathbf{Regular}, by Theorem 13.1, there is a DFA B s.t. \mathscr{L}(B)=L'. Due to Theorem 19.2, to prove the result it enough to construct a PDA C s.t. \mathscr{L}(C)=L\cap L'. The construction of C follows the same idea used for the cartesian product construction we saw in Example 9.7.





Exercise 19.6 Fill the details of the proof sketch of Theorem 19.3.


Theorem 19.4 The inverse image of a context-free language under a homomorphism is context-free.






For the proof of this fact see (Hopcroft et al. 2007, Thorem 7.30).

title: 19  Pushdown Automata
text:
19.3 \mathbf{DCFL} – Deterministic Context-Free Languages
In this section we recall properties of deterministic PDAs. Intuitively, similarly to DFAs, a PDA is deterministic when there are never options for the transitions to take. In other words, if for every q\in Q and instantaneous description \mathrm{ID}=(q,x,\alpha) there is at most one instantaneous description \mathrm{ID}' s.t. \mathrm{ID}\vdash_A\mathrm{ID}'.

Definition 19.3 (\mathbf{DCFL} – Deterministic Context-Free Languages) A CFL L is deterministic if there exist a deterministic pushdown automata A s.t. \mathscr{L}(A)=L. \mathbf{DCFL} is the set of all deterministic context-free languages (over a fixed alphabet).

The interest in \mathbf{DCFL} is practical: parsing for languages in \mathbf{DCFL} can be done in linear time.

Exercise 19.7 Is the PDA in Figure 19.3 deterministic?


Exercise 19.8 Is the PDA you constructed in Exercise 19.3 deterministic?

Exercise 19.10 (🔥) Show that \mathbf{DCFL} is closed under complement and use this fact to conclude that \mathbf{DCFL}\subsetneq \mathbf{CFL}.






Warning



The obvious construction of interchanging final and non-final states does not work immediately. The point is that a deterministic pushdown automata is close to a DFA but not exactly!

title: 21  Limitations of CFL
text:
21.1 The Pumping Lemma for Context-Free Languages
In this chapter we see some techniques to show that a language is not context free and we will use them to show that \mathbf{CFL} is not closed under intersection and complement.
For regular languages, a prototypical example of language not in \mathbf{Regular} was \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n :n \in \mathbb{N}\}. For context-free languages, a prototypical example of language not in \mathbf{CFL} is \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{c}}^n :n \in \mathbb{N}\}.
In the case of regular languages just from the fact that \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n :n \in \mathbb{N}\}\notin \mathbf{Regular} and using closure properties of regular languages we can obtain several results. Here we are in a similar situation. We can use the fact that \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{c}}^n :n \in \mathbb{N}\}\notin \mathbf{CFL} and closure properties of context-free languages to obtain several results (see Section 21.2 for more examples).
The proof of Theorem 21.2 does not explicitly provide an example of a context-free language whose complement is not context-free. An example of such a language is the complement of \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{c}}^n :n \in \mathbb{N}\} (see Exercise 22.1).
The argument used to prove Example 21.1 can be abstracted to the following statement which is known as the pumping lemma for context-free languages. The proof in Example 21.1 constructs a pumping length n=2^N for this particular grammar; the abstract lemma packages this argument into an arbitrary pumping length n.
As for the pumping lemma for regular languages (Lemma 14.1), the use of the pumping lemma for context-free languages is essentially describing a winning strategy for the following game. Given a language we want to prove is not context-free:
Hence a “template” for a proof using the pumping lemma for context-free languages is as follow:
Although the overall structure is similar, usually applications of the pumping-lemma for context-free languages (Lemma 21.1) require a more detailed case analysis than the pumping lemma for regular languages (Lemma 14.1). This typically leads to quite “inelegant” proofs, and as in the case of regular languages often it is possible to prove the non-context-freeness of languages using closure properties and the known fact that some notable language is not context-free.

21  Limitations of CFL
21  Limitations of CFL
text:
21.3 Inherently ambiguous languages
Often, for context-free languages, we can provide a non-ambiguous grammar generating them. This is not always the case.

Theorem 21.3 Every CFG generating \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^m\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{c}}^m :n,m\in \mathbb{N}\}\cup \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{a}}^m\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{b}}^m\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{c}}^n :n,m\in \mathbb{N}\} is ambiguous.


Theorem 21.4 Every CFG generating \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^m\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^m :n,m\in \mathbb{N}\}\cup \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^n\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^m\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^m\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^n :n,m\in \mathbb{N}\} is ambiguous.

These results above justify the existence of the class of all inherently ambiguous context-free languages, that is all context-free languages with the property that every CFG generating them is ambiguous.
Figure 1 shows how the inherently ambiguous CFL fit w.r.t. other classes of languages.

Exercise 21.8 Show that DCFL is not contained into the inherently ambiguous CFL, and viceversa.

We do not prove Theorem 21.3 nor Theorem 21.4, but we only mention that they both can be proved using a generalization of Lemma 21.1 known as the Ogden Lemma, which (informally) allows to select zones to pump.
