title: 23  Turing Machines
text:
23.1 TMs as a “programming language”
Finite automata are a good model for machines that have access to a small amount of memory, PDAs for machines that have access to an unlimited memory but in the form of a stack. We also saw limitations of those devices.
In this chapter we develop the model we use for a general purpouse computer: the Turing machine.
A Turing machine (somewhat informally) is a finite states machine with an initial state q_{0}, two halting states q_{\mathrm{accept}} and q_{\mathrm{reject}}. The machine apart from its states has reading/writing access to a tape and has transitions of the form
The intended meaning of such transition is
Similarly, a transition of the form q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\to q',\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{t}}, L would be the same as before but now the head moves to the Left, and a transition of the form q,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{s}}\to q',\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{t}}, S would be the same as before but now the head does not move.
At the beginning of the computation the machine is in its start configuration: the machine is in the initial state q_0, the head is on the cell 1, the input to the machine is written on the tape in the leftmost consecutive cells. That is between \blacktriangleright and the first empty cell, a cell containing -.
Given two configurations C=(q,t,\ell) and D=(q',t',\ell') we say that C yields D (denoted as C\vdash_M D) if either
A configuration is accepting if the state of the configuration is q_{\mathrm{accept}}, and, similarly, a configuration is rejecting if the state of the configuration is q_{\mathrm{reject}}. A configuration is halting if it does not yield further configurations. Both q_{\mathrm{accept}} and q_{\mathrm{reject}} are halting configurations by definition.
For example, Figure 23.3, corresponds to a TM starting the execution on input \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1011}}.
Given a Turing machine M and an input x, there are thre possibilities for the behaviour of M(x) (M on input x):
A Turing machine is a very low-level programming language. If you look at its transition table the right way, it is an assembly program with goto:
High-level languages are compiled down to gotos, and we can do the same with Turing machines.
In this section we show how to implement the basic constructs of pseudo-code: sequential composition, if-then-else, while and for loops, variables and subroutines. Once that is done, we can describe Turing machines by pseudo-code and trust that a transition table could be written if needed.
To compose machines, we stop thinking of a TM as something that accepts or rejects, and instead think of it as a block of code:
An ordinary TM is just a block whose exit states are q_{\mathrm{accept}} and q_{\mathrm{reject}}. Blocks with two exits, say yes and no, are tests: they play the role of Boolean conditions.
Two blocks used together must have disjoint sets of state names; if they don’t, we rename states (for instance by adding a prefix, A.q0, B.q0, …). Renaming states does not change what a block does.
Throughout, we draw blocks as boxes:

title: 23  Turing Machines
text:
the states are the program points (the “line numbers” or labels);
a transition q a -> p b D says: “at label q, if you read a, write b, move D, then goto p”;
the tape is the memory.









TipConventions



We use the same notation as before: > denotes the left-end marker \blacktriangleright, _ is the blank, and moves are L, R, S (stay). A missing transition means reject.
To keep tables short, we use a wildcard: * stands for “any symbol not handled by another rule for that state”, and writing * on both sides means “write back the same symbol”. So
r * -> r * R
is an abbreviation for one transition r a -> r a R for every tape symbol a.




Definition 23.4 (Block) A block is a Turing machine fragment with

one entry state (where control enters), and
one or more exit states (where control leaves), which have no outgoing transitions inside the block.











Figure 23.4




23.1.1 Sequential composition: M1 ; M2
To run M1 and then M2: identify the exit state of M1 with the entry state of M2.






Figure 23.5




Example 23.2 Let’s see for example an implementation of “go to the right end, then come back to the left end” Block GoRight (entry r, exit rdone):
r * -> r * R
r _ -> rdone _ L      # last symbol of the word
Block GoLeft (entry l, exit ldone):
l * -> l * L
l > -> ldone > R      # first symbol of the word
GoRight ; GoLeft is obtained by renaming rdone to l:
r * -> r * R
r _ -> l _ L
l * -> l * L
l > -> ldone > R

The only thing to watch is that M2 must work correctly starting from wherever M1 left the head. This is the TM version of a precondition. In practice, many blocks are written to start and end with the head on the first symbol of the word, so they can be chained freely.


23.1.2 Conditionals: if T then M1 else M2
Let T be a test with exits yes and no. To build the conditional:

identify yes with the entry of M1;
identify no with the entry of M2;
identify the exits of M1 and M2 with a common exit state.







Figure 23.6




Example 23.3 Let’s see a way to implement “if the current symbol is 0 then write 1 else write 0” (flip a bit) The test only looks at the current cell and does not move:
t 0 -> yes 0 S
t 1 -> no 1 S
Then and else branches:
yes 0 -> done 1 S
no 1 -> done 0 S
After simplifying (a test followed immediately by a write can be merged into one transition), we get the expected one-state machine:
t 0 -> done 1 S
t 1 -> done 0 S

Conditions can be more complicated than “what symbol is under the head”: a test can be any block with two exits, e.g. “is the word a palindrome?”. The one rule is that a test should leave the tape in a known state (typically: content unchanged, head back where it started), so that both branches know what they start from.


23.1.3 While loops: while T do B
Identify:

yes with the entry of B;
the exit of B with the entry of T (this is the “jump back”);
no with the exit of the loop.







Figure 23.7




Example 23.4 Let’s implement the following “while the current symbol is not >, move left” Test (does not move):
w > -> no > S
w * -> yes * S
Body (one step left, then jump back to the test):
yes * -> w * L
Merging test and body gives exactly the GoLeft block we already saw:
w * -> w * L
w > -> no > S

So the “go back to the left end” loops found in almost every TM are while loops. Note that a while loop can run forever: this is precisely how Turing machines can fail to halt.


23.1.4 Variables
If a variable can only take values from a finite set V (a Boolean flag, a counter modulo 3, the last symbol read, …), we can store it in the finite control: replace each state q by the pairs (q, v) with v \in V. This multiplies the number of states by |V|, which is still finite.
Variables whose values are unbounded (numbers, words) are stored on the tape. Two standard layouts:

Several tapes. A k-tape TM has one tape per variable; each transition reads and writes k symbols and moves k heads. One can prove that every k-tape TM can be simulated by a 1-tape TM (with a quadratic slowdown), so using several tapes does not change what is computable.
Separators. On a single tape, store the variables one after another, separated by a fresh symbol:

\blacktriangleright\; x_1 \;\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}}\; x_2 \;\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}}\; \cdots \;\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}}\; x_k \;\texttt{\_}
 To “access x_i”, go to the left end and skip i-1 separators \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}}.

With variables on the tape, the usual operations become blocks: copy x := y, increment x := x + 1 (the binary increment machine), compare x = y (a test), and so on.


23.1.5 For loops: for i = 1 to n do B
A for loop is a while loop over a counter stored on the tape. The simplest version uses a unary counter: the tape is \blacktriangleright\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^n\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}}\,w, and each iteration crosses off one \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}.
for each 1 in the counter:
    cross it off
    run B
As a while loop: while there is an uncrossed \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}} in the counter, cross it off, run B, go back to the left end.

Example 23.5 Let’s see for example a loop control around a body B We assume that B has entry B.start and exit B.done, does not modify the counter, and does not need the head in any particular place when it starts.
c x -> c x R             # skip the 1s already crossed off
c 1 -> B.start x S       # cross off one 1, then run the body
c # -> exit # S          # no 1 left: the loop is over

# ... the transitions of B, from B.start to B.done ...

B.done * -> back * L     # after the body: go back to the left end
back * -> back * L
back > -> c > R          # and test again

With a binary counter, use the same scheme with the test “is the counter 0?” and the body “decrement the counter; run B”. The decrement machine is the mirror image of the binary increment machine.
Unlike a while loop, a for loop always terminates provided its body does, because the counter strictly decreases.


23.1.6 Subroutines
A subroutine call is handled like a macro: we paste a fresh copy of the subroutine’s block (with renamed states) at each call site, and wire it in with sequential composition.
This works because a program has only finitely many call sites, so the result still has finitely many states.






WarningRecursion



Pasting copies does not work for recursive subroutines, since that would produce infinitely many copies. Recursion needs an explicit stack stored on the tape (for example on an extra tape), exactly like a compiler implements recursion with a call stack in memory. This is possible, but tedious, and we will not need it.

title: 25  The Church-Turing Thesis
text:
25.1 Computable functions
In this chapter we focus on formalizing the informal notion of computable function, the Universal Turing machine and the Gödel numbering of Turing machines.
For several reasons at the beginning of the 20th century mathematicians and logicians started to be interested in the concept of computation, more concretely what types of functions f\colon \mathbb{N}^k \to \mathbb{N} can be computed by means of an algorithm, i.e. “a process according to which the value of f(\vec x) can be determined from \vec x by a finite number of operations”.
To model this informal notion of computation logicians used different models of what it could mean to compute, including
Despite the different formalisms, it turned out that all those models give rise to exactly the same class of functions f\colon \mathbb{N}^k \to \mathbb{N} that can be computed. The Church-Turing thesis is this: the intuitive notion of algorithm can be captured by any of the formal models of computation above. We use the Turing machines.
The only difference between the two definitions is that to define a computable function from \mathbb{N}^k to \mathbb{N}, we used an encoding of tuples of natural numbers. For simplicity we used \Sigma=\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\} and a unary encoding for numbers n\mapsto \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^n, and \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}} as a separator.

title: 25  The Church-Turing Thesis
25  The Church-Turing Thesis
text:
25.2 Universal Turing Machine
The Universal Turing Machine (UTM) is Turing’s all-purpose computing machine. The universal machine is able to emulate the behavior of any single-purpose Turing machine, i.e., any Turing machine set up to solve one particular problem. The universal machine does this by means of storing a description of the other machine on its tape, in the form of a finite list of instructions (a computer program, in modern terms). By following suitable instructions, the universal machine can carry out any and every effective procedure, assuming the Church-Turing’s thesis is true.
In that respect, the universal Turing machine is a bare-bones logical model of almost every modern electronic digital computer.
The existence of an UTM follows from the Church-Turing thesis:

The process of “simulating a specific Turing machine M given its description and input” is itself an algorithmic, effectively calculable process (a human clerk or a systematic procedure could read the rules of M and step through them).
By the Church-Turing thesis, any effectively calculable procedure must be computable by some Turing machine.
Therefore, there must exist a Turing machine U that can perform this simulation—which is precisely the definition of the universal Turing machine.

The argument above is informal because it appeals to the Church-Turing thesis, but the existence of the UTM is actually a formal theorem (we omit the proof).

Theorem 25.1 (Universal Turing Machine) There exist a Turing machine U s.t. on input \langle M\rangle (any reasonable encoding of a Turing machine M) and a word x, simulates the execution of M with input x, that is if M with input x

accepts and writes on the tape y, then U with input \langle M\rangle,x accepts and writes on the tape y;
rejects, then U with input \langle M\rangle,x rejects;
does not terminate, then U with input \langle M\rangle,x does not terminate.

title: 25  The Church-Turing Thesis
text:
25.3 Encoding of Turing machines
A Turing machine is a finite object, so you can write it down as a string, and any string can be read as a number. The Gödel number of a Turing machine is just its “source code” read as a number.






TipSlogan



Programs are data. Every Turing machine is a finite string and every string is a number. So we can list all machines as M_0, M_1, M_2, \dots, and machines can take other machines’ numbers as input.


A simple way to encode a Turing machine as a number is as follows:
1. Normalize the machine. Rename the states q_1, \dots, q_n, with q_1 the start state, q_2 the accepting state and q_3 the rejecting state. Rename the tape symbols s_1, \dots, s_m, with s_1 the blank and s_2=\blacktriangleright. Name the directions D_1 = L, D_2 = R, and D_3=S. Renaming doesn’t change what the machine computes.
2. Write each transition as a \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}/\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}} string. Write a transition \delta(q_i, s_j) = (q_k, s_l, D_r) as 
\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^i\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^j\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^k\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^l\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}^r .
 Every field is a positive number of \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}s, so a single \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}} separates fields without ambiguity.

Example 25.1 The transition \delta(q_1, s_3) = (q_2, s_2, R) becomes 
\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0\;1\;000\;1\;00\;1\;00\;1\;00}} .


3. Glue the transitions together. List the transitions C_1, \dots, C_t in any order and separate them with \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{11}}:

\langle M \rangle = C_1\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{11}}\,C_2\,\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{11}}\cdots \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{11}}\,C_t .
 Read \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\langle M\rangle as a binary number. The extra leading \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}} keeps the leading zeros from getting lost. That number is the Gödel number of M.
Some key properties of the Gödel numbering are the following:

Every machine gets a number. A machine can get several numbers, one per ordering of its transitions, but that never matters.
Coding and decoding are computable. Given p \in \mathbb{N}, a Turing machine can check whether p is a valid code and, if it is, rebuild the transition table. This is what makes a universal machine possible.
Every number names a machine. Use the convention that if p is not a valid code, M_p is a fixed trivial machine, e.g. one that never halts. This gives a list 
M_0,\ M_1,\ M_2,\ \dots
 of all Turing machines. We write \varphi_p for the (partial) function computed by M_p.







NoteRemark: Gödel’s original approach





Gödel encoded sequences with prime powers, 2^{a_1}3^{a_2}5^{a_3}\cdots. That works the same way, but the string-then-binary version fits better with the view of computable functions as functions on \Sigma^*.



With the language of a Gödel numbering of Turing machines, Theorem 25.1 can be also written as follows.

Theorem 25.2 (Universal Turing Machine) There exist a Turing machine U s.t. for every p,x\in \mathbb{N}1 U(p,x)=M_p(x).

title: 26  \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{RE}, \mathbf{coRE} and beyond
text:
26.1 The Arithmetical Hierarchy
In this chapter we introduce the classes of languages \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{RE}, and \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE} (for the meaning of the \mathbf{co} prefix see Equation 26.1) and we prove some basic properties of them.
Recall that for a Turing machine M and input x,
The previous definitions adapt naturally to L\subseteq \mathbb{N} identifying the natural numbers with strings in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}\}\cup\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}^* via the binary encoding.
The opposite containment of Exercise 26.1 is also true.
The argument used in the proof above is called diagonalization and it is essentially the same idea we saw in Chapter 3. Visually, the table below highlights visually the argument in the proof of Theorem 26.2.
The fact that \mathtt{K}\notin \mathbf{R} is a fact that we will exploit in a systematic way to show that many more natural languages are not in \mathbf{R} either (see Chapter 27).
In this section we explore a bit what is beyond \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{RE}, and \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}. To do so we prove first a logical characterization of \mathbf{RE} and \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}.
To make sure you understood the proof of Theorem 26.3 a possible exercise is the following.
An immediate consequence of Theorem 26.3 is the following.
Theorem 26.3 says that the languages in \mathbf{RE} are exactly the languages obtained from a decidable language by putting an existential quantifier in front. The arithmetical hierarchy repeats this construction, adding one quantifier at each level and switching between existential and universal quantifiers. This hierarchy classifies subsets of natural numbers based on the complexity of formulas defining them.
For a class of languages \mathcal{C}, we define 
\mathbf{co}\mathcal{C}=\{A:\overline A\in\mathcal{C}\}.
\tag{26.1}
By Theorem 26.1, we have that \mathbf{R}=\Delta^0_1, and unfolding Definition 26.4 gives each level as a block of alternating quantifiers in front of a decidable language. Several quantifiers of the same kind in a row can be merged into one quantifier over tuples, as in Theorem 26.3.
The inclusion in the previous exercise is actually strict, and Exercise 27.4 asks to prove this (for k=1).
At first sight the arithmetical hierarchy might look a bit artificial, but, as the following exercise shows, some languages are naturally in higher classes than \mathbf{RE} or \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}.
We do not see the proof of Theorem 26.6, but it is a generalization of the diagonal argument we used in Theorem 26.2.
Putting together all the containments between \Delta^0_k and \Sigma^0_k and \Pi^0_k we obtain Figure 26.1, which is part of the big picture in Figure 1.

title: 26  \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{RE}, \mathbf{coRE} and beyond
text:
There is an equivalent way of describing the arithmetical hierarchy using oracle Turing machines and the Turing jump operator. In these notes we do not explore this equivalent view.

Theorem 26.3 A language A\in \mathbf{RE} if and only if there exists a language B\in \mathbf{R} s.t. A=\{y:\exists x_1,\dots,x_n \langle x_1,\dots,x_n,y\rangle\in B\}.






NoteProof





(\Rightarrow) Let A\in\mathbf{RE} and let M be a Turing machine that recognizes A, i.e. \mathscr{L}(M)=A. Define 
B=\{\langle t,y\rangle :M \text{ accepts } y \text{ within } t \text{ steps}\}.
 B\in\mathbf{R}: on input \langle t,y\rangle, simulate M on y for at most t steps. Accept if M has accepted by then, otherwise reject. This always halts. Moreover,

y\in A \iff M \text{ accepts } y \iff \exists t\ \langle t,y\rangle\in B,
 so A has the required form with n=1.
(\Leftarrow) Let B\in\mathbf{R} be decided by a Turing machine D that always halts, and let A=\{y:\exists x_1,\dots,x_n\ \langle x_1,\dots,x_n,y\rangle\in B\}. Tuples (x_1,\dots,x_n) of strings can be listed effectively, e.g. by going through all strings w in length-lexicographic order1 and keeping those that encode a tuple. Consider the machine M that, on input y, goes through this list and for each tuple (x_1,\dots,x_n) runs D on \langle x_1,\dots,x_n,y\rangle. It accepts as soon as D accepts.
Each run of D halts, so M never gets stuck on a single tuple. If y\in A, the tuple that witnesses this shows up after finitely many steps and M accepts. If y\notin A, D never accepts and M never accepts (it runs forever). So \mathscr{L}(M)=A and A\in\mathbf{RE}.






Exercise 26.4 Let \Sigma=\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\} and n=2. In the (\Leftarrow) direction of the theorem above (Theorem 26.3), suppose we change the machine M so that it goes through the pairs (x_1,x_2) with two nested loops:
On input y:
    for each x_1\in\Sigma^* in length-lexicographic order {
        for each x_2\in\Sigma^* in length-lexicographic order {
            run D on \langle x_1,x_2,y\rangle
            if D accepts then
                  return accept
          }
      }


Find a language B\in\mathbf{R} and a string y\in A such that the M above does not accept y.
Explain why this does not contradict the theorem, and give an ordering of \Sigma^*\times\Sigma^* (different from the one in the theorem) that fixes the problem.




Theorem 26.4 A language A\in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE} if and only if there exists a language B\in \mathbf{R} s.t. A=\{y:\forall x_1,\dots,x_n \langle x_1,\dots,x_n,y\rangle\in B\}.


Exercise 26.5 Prove Theorem 26.4 using the definition of \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE} and Theorem 26.3.


Example 26.1 The language

\mathtt{ALL_{CFG}}=\{\langle G\rangle :G \text{ is a context-free grammar and } \mathscr{L}(G)=\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}^*\}
 is in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}.
A simple way to see this is to use Theorem 26.4. The property “G is a context-free grammar and \mathscr{L}(G)=\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}^*” can indeed be written as “\forall w\in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}^*, G is a context-free grammar whose terminals are in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\} and G generates w”. The condition on the terminals guarantees \mathscr{L}(G)\subseteq\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}^*, and the universal quantifier guarantees \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}^*\subseteq\mathscr{L}(G). Now, “G is a context-free grammar whose terminals are in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}” is clearly decidable (it is a syntactic check) and “G generates w” is also decidable (for example using the CYK algorithm we saw in Section 17.1). Hence \mathtt{ALL_{CFG}} has the form of languages in Theorem 26.4, with B=\{\langle G,w\rangle :G \text{ is a context-free grammar whose terminals are in } \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\} \text{ and } G \text{ generates } w\}. We just argued that B\in \mathbf{R}.
A true (but not obvious) fact is that \mathtt{ALL_{CFG}}\notin\mathbf{R}.


Exercise 26.6 Show that the language

\mathtt{EMPTY_{CFG}}=\{\langle G_1, G_2\rangle :G_1, G_2 \text{ CFGs and } \mathscr{L}(G_1)\cap\mathscr{L}(G_2)=\emptyset\}
 is in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}. In other words, \mathtt{EMPTY_{CFG}} is the language of valid encodings of two context-free grammars with empty intersection of the generated languages.
(As before, a true, but not obvious fact is that \mathtt{EMPTY_{CFG}}\notin\mathbf{R}.)




Definition 26.4 (\Sigma^0_k, \Pi^0_k, \Delta^0_k) The classes \Sigma^0_k, \Pi^0_k and \Delta^0_k, for k\geqslant 1, are defined recursively as follows. \Sigma^0_1:=\mathbf{RE}, \Pi^0_1:=\mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}, and for k\geqslant 1,

A\in\Sigma^0_{k+1} if there exists a language B\in\Pi^0_k such that
A=\{y:\exists x\ \langle x,y\rangle\in B\};
\Pi^0_{k+1}:=\mathbf{co}\Sigma^0_{k+1};
\Delta^0_k:=\Sigma^0_k\cap\Pi^0_k.




Why the superscript 0? The superscript says what the quantifiers range over: individual objects, such as natural numbers or strings, called “type-0” objects in logic. With quantifiers over sets of natural numbers (type-1 objects) we get the analytical hierarchy \Sigma^1_k,\Pi^1_k, which is much larger. Complexity theory uses the same idea in the polynomial hierarchy \Sigma^p_k,\Pi^p_k, where the quantifiers range over strings of polynomial length.


Theorem 26.5 A\in\Sigma^0_k if and only if there exists a language B\in\mathbf{R} such that 
A=\{y:\exists x_1\,\forall x_2\,\exists x_3\cdots Q_k x_k\ \langle x_1,\dots,x_k,y\rangle\in B\},
 where Q_k is \exists if k is odd and \forall if k is even. Similarly, A\in\Pi^0_k if and only if A has the same form with the quantifiers starting from \forall x_1.


Exercise 26.7 (🌱) Prove that \Delta^0_1=\mathbf{R}.


Exercise 26.8 Prove that \Sigma^0_k\cup\Pi^0_k\subseteq\Delta^0_{k+1}.




Exercise 26.9 Show the following:

\mathtt{FIN}=\{p:\mathscr{L}(M_p) \text{ is finite}\}\in\Sigma^0_2.
\mathtt{TOT}=\{p:M_p \text{ halts on every input}\}\in\Pi^0_2.



Theorem 26.6 \Delta^0_k\subsetneq \Sigma^0_k.



Exercise 26.10 This exercise asks to show a couple of consequences of Theorem 26.6.

\Delta^0_k\subsetneq \Pi^0_k.
\Sigma^0_k\not\subseteq \Pi^0_k and \Pi^0_k\not\subseteq \Sigma^0_k.









Scheme of the containments between classes in the arithmetical hierarchy. \mathcal C \to \mathcal D with a black arrow means that \mathcal C\subsetneq \mathcal D (that is \mathcal C\subseteq \mathcal D and the inclusion is strict). A red dashed line means that neither of the containments holds.

title: 27  Many-One Reductions
text:
27.1 A workflow to decide whether L\in \mathbf{R},\mathbf{RE}\setminus\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}\setminus\mathbf{R}, \dots
In this chapter we see how to prove that many languages are not in \mathbf{R}. Informally, this is done by “reducing” the problem of showing that a language L is not in \mathbf{R}, by showing that \mathtt{K} or some other language we already know is not in \mathbf{R} is “easier” than our language L. Formally, this is done using the concept of many-one reductions.
Recall that f\colon\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^* is a total computable function s.t. there is a Turing machine M where for every input x\in \Sigma^*, M(x) halts, accepts and has on the tape f(x).
If A\leqslant_m B, then A is “no harder” than B: to decide whether x\in A, compute f(x) and ask whether f(x)\in B. The following properties follow directly from the definition.
Item 3 is usually used in the contrapositive: to show that B\notin\mathbf{R}, reduce a known undecidable language to B. Note the direction: the known hard language goes on the left.
Let’s see now another (more interesting) example.
In the RACSO page you have several examples of many-one reductions but be aware that not all interesting reductions to \mathtt{K} or \overline{\mathtt{K}} can be written using the language in the RACSO page.
One example of reduction that cannot be done using the language of RACSO is the following:
Given a language L we now have all the tools to show whether L\in \mathbf{R}, or L\in \mathbf{RE}\setminus\mathbf{R}, or L\in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}\setminus\mathbf{R}, or L\in \Sigma^0_2\setminus (\mathbf{RE}\cup\mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}) (you also need to show that L\in \Sigma^0_2 for the upper bound), etc.
Similarly to the exercise above, we have that for every k there exists a language L\in \Delta^0_{k+1}\setminus (\Sigma^0_k\cup\Pi^0_k) for every k\geqslant 1.

title: 27  Many-One Reductions
text:
L\in \mathbf{R}L\in \mathbf{RE}\setminus\mathbf{R}L\in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}\setminus\mathbf{R}L\notin \mathbf{RE}\cup\mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}


Usually the simplest thing is to describe a Turing machine or algorithm to decide L.


First show that L\in \mathbf{RE} either constructing a Turing machine that semi-decides L or use Theorem 26.3. Then prove that A\leqslant_m L for some language A\notin\mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}, for example showing that \mathtt{K}\leqslant_m L.


First show that L\in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE} either constructing a Turing machine that semi-decides \overline L or use Theorem 26.4. Then prove that A\leqslant_m L for some language A\notin\mathbf{RE}, for example showing that \overline{\mathtt{K}}\leqslant_m L.


Prove that A\leqslant_m L and B\leqslant_m L for some A\notin \mathbf{RE} and B\notin \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}, for example K and \overline{K}.




Exercise 27.3 In this exercise we continue on Exercise 26.9. Show that

\mathtt{FIN}=\{p:\mathscr{L}(M_p) \text{ is finite}\}\in\Sigma^0_2\setminus (\mathbf{RE}\cup\mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}).
\mathtt{TOT}=\{p:M_p \text{ halts on every input}\}\in\Pi^0_2\setminus (\mathbf{RE}\cup\mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}).



Exercise 27.4 Consider the language

A=\mathtt{K}\oplus\overline{\mathtt{K}}=\{\langle 0,z\rangle:z\in\mathtt{K}\}\cup\{\langle 1,z\rangle:z\notin\mathtt{K}\}.
 Show that A\in\Delta^0_2 but A\notin\mathbf{RE}\cup\mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}.

title: 28  More Exercises
text:
Important



The explanations of wrong anwers are partially generated using AI tools. Please report any error.



Exercise 28.1 (A complement of a union)  

Let A, B and C be languages such that A \in \mathbf{RE}\setminus \mathbf{R} and A = \overline{B \cup C}. Which of the following options for B and C is not possible?




A. B \in \mathbf{RE} and C \in \mathbf{RE}


\mathbf{RE} is closed under union, so B \cup C \in \mathbf{RE}. But B \cup C = \overline{A}, so \overline{A} \in \mathbf{RE}, which means A \in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}. Together with A \in \mathbf{RE}, this gives A \in \mathbf{RE}\cap \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}= \mathbf{R}, contradicting A \notin \mathbf{R}. So this option is impossible.




B. B \in \mathbf{RE} or C \in \mathbf{RE}


This is possible. Take B = \emptyset and C = \overline{A}. Then \overline{B \cup C} = A, and B = \emptyset \in \mathbf{RE}. Only one of the two languages has to be in \mathbf{RE}, so the argument for the correct answer does not apply.




C. B \in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE} or C \in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}


This is possible. Since A \in \mathbf{RE}, its complement \overline{A} is in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}. Take B = \overline{A} and C = \emptyset. Then \overline{B \cup C} = A, and B \in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}.




D. B \in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE} and C \in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}


This is possible. Take again B = \overline{A} \in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE} and C = \emptyset, which is in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE} because it is decidable. Then \overline{B \cup C} = A. This is consistent: \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE} is closed under union, and indeed B \cup C = \overline{A} \in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}.





Exercise 28.2 (Twin primes)  

Let 
L = \{\, n \in \mathbb{N} :\exists p \geqslant n \text{ such that } p \text{ and } p+2 \text{ are both prime} \,\}.
 Which is the strongest statement you can guarantee for sure to be true?




A. L \in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}


This is true, but it follows from a stronger statement (see the correct answer). Note that it is not obvious directly: to reject n, we would have to be sure that there are no twin primes beyond n, and no search can confirm that. The point is that L is decidable, and every decidable language is in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}. The best answer is the strongest one we can guarantee.




B. L \in \mathbf{RE}


This is true: on input n, search p = n, n+1, n+2, \dots and accept when p and p+2 are both prime. If n \in L, the search ends. But this only shows L \in \mathbf{RE}, and we can say more: L is decidable (see the correct answer). The best answer is the strongest one we can guarantee.




C. L \in \mathbf{R}


L is closed downwards: if n \in L and m \leqslant n, then m \in L. So there are only two possibilities. If there are infinitely many twin primes, then L = \mathbb{N}. Otherwise, let p_0 be the largest prime such that p_0 + 2 is also prime, and then L = \{0, 1, \dots, p_0\}. In both cases, L is decidable: \mathbb{N} is decided by a machine that always accepts, and \{0, \dots, p_0\} by a machine that compares n with the constant p_0. We do not know which of these machines decides L, because the twin prime conjecture is open, but we know that one of them does. Decidability asks for the existence of a decider, not for us to know which one it is.




D. L \notin \mathbf{RE}\cup \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}


This is false. As explained in the correct answer, L is either \mathbb{N} or a finite set, and in both cases L \in \mathbf{R}\subseteq \mathbf{RE}\cap \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}.





Exercise 28.3 (Which statement is false?)  

Which of the following statements about languages A, B \subseteq \{0,1\}^* is false?




A. If A = \mathcal{L}(M) where M is a Turing machine that does not halt on 010, then A \in \mathbf{RE}\setminus \mathbf{R}.


This statement is false. The fact that one particular machine M for A does not halt does not mean that every machine for A fails to halt. For example, let M accept every word except 010, and loop forever on 010. Then A = \mathcal{L}(M) = \{0,1\}^* \setminus \{010\}. This language is decidable: another machine can check whether its input is 010 and reject it, and accept everything else. So A \in \mathbf{R}. Decidability is a property of the language, not of one machine that recognizes it.




B. If A \notin \mathbf{R}, then A \cup \{0101\} \notin \mathbf{R}.


This statement is true. Suppose A \cup \{0101\} were decidable, with decider D. Then A would also be decidable. If 0101 \in A, then A = A \cup \{0101\}. If 0101 \notin A, then A = (A \cup \{0101\}) \setminus \{0101\}, which is decided by running D and rejecting 0101. We may not know which case holds, but in both cases a decider for A exists, contradicting A \notin \mathbf{R}. Changing a language on finitely many words never affects decidability.




C. If A \notin \mathbf{R} and B is finite, then A \cup B \notin \mathbf{R}.


This statement is true. It is the previous statement with \{0101\} replaced by any finite set. If A \cup B were decidable, then A = (A \cup B) \setminus (B \setminus A) would be decidable too, because B \setminus A is finite and a decider can store the finitely many words of B \setminus A and reject them.




D. If A \in \mathbf{RE}, there are infinitely many Turing machines that recognize A.


This statement is true. If M recognizes A, we can add any number of new states that are never reached, and we obtain infinitely many different machines that all recognize A. This is the same padding trick that gives every machine infinitely many encodings, which we use in the proof of the time hierarchy theorem.





Exercise 28.4 (Right-moving Turing machines (Partial exam 2, 05/06/2026))  

A Turing machine is called right-moving if its head can never move to the left or stay in the same position (that is, it can only move to the right). What is the class of languages accepted by right-moving Turing machines?




A. The languages in \mathbf{P}.


\mathbf{P} contains non-regular languages such as \{0^n 1^n :n \geqslant 0\}, which a right-moving TM cannot accept. Such a machine reads each input symbol exactly once, from left to right, and can never come back to anything it has written. So the only memory it has is its finite set of states, and it cannot count the 0s in order to compare them with the 1s.




B. The context-free languages.


A right-moving TM cannot even accept the context-free language \{0^n 1^n :n \geqslant 0\}. Unlike a pushdown automaton, it has no stack: everything it writes is left behind, to the left of the head, and it can never read it again. Its only memory is its finite set of states.




C. The recursive languages.


Being able to move left is essential for a TM to use its tape as memory. A right-moving TM reads each input symbol once and never revisits a cell, so it behaves like a finite automaton. It cannot accept non-regular decidable languages such as \{0^n 1^n :n \geqslant 0\}.




D. The regular languages.


A right-moving TM scans its input from left to right, one symbol per step, and whatever it writes lands in cells it will never visit again. So its behaviour depends only on its current state and the current input symbol, exactly like a DFA. After the input, it only reads blanks, and its behaviour from then on depends only on the state in which it left the input, so a DFA can tell in advance whether it will eventually accept. Conversely, every DFA is a right-moving TM. Hence right-moving TMs accept exactly the regular languages.





Exercise 28.5 (Where a machine does not halt (Partial exam 2, 05/06/2026))  

Let M be a Turing machine, let A = \mathcal{L}(M) be the language recognized by M, and let B = \{w :M(w)\uparrow\} be the set of words on which M does not halt. Which of the following statements is false for some M?
Recall that \mathbf{R} is the class of all decidable languages, and that a set S is cofinite if \overline{S} is finite.




A. If B is cofinite, then A \in \mathbf{R}.


This statement is always true. M can only accept words on which it halts, so A \subseteq \overline{B}. If B is cofinite, then \overline{B} is finite, so A is finite, and every finite language is decidable.




B. If B is finite, then A \in \mathbf{R}.


This statement is always true. If B is finite, a decider for A can store the finitely many words of B. On input w, it rejects if w \in B, because M does not halt on w and so does not accept it. Otherwise, it simulates M on w, which is guaranteed to halt, and gives the same answer.




C. A \in \mathbf{RE} independently of B.


This statement is always true. By definition, A = \mathcal{L}(M) is recognized by the Turing machine M, so A \in \mathbf{RE}, whatever B is.




D. If B is infinite, then A \in \mathbf{R}.


This statement fails for some M. Let K = \{p :M_p(p)\downarrow\}. Then K \in \mathbf{RE}, so K = \mathcal{L}(M) for some TM M, and we can take A = K. We know that K \notin \mathbf{R}. Moreover, B is infinite: there are infinitely many programs p with M_p(p)\uparrow, and on each of them M does not halt. So B is infinite but A \notin \mathbf{R}.





Exercise 28.6 (Programs with finite image (Partial exam 2, 05/06/2026))  

Consider the language L = \{\, p :\mathrm{Im}(\varphi_p) \text{ is finite} \,\}, where \varphi_p is the function computed by the program p. Which of the following is true?




A. L \in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}\setminus \mathbf{R}


L is not in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}, because K \leqslant_m L. Given x, build a program p_x that, on input y, outputs 1 if M_x(x) halts within |y| steps, and outputs y otherwise. If M_x(x)\downarrow in t steps, then p_x outputs 1 on all inputs of length at least t, so its image is finite. If M_x(x)\uparrow, then p_x computes the identity, whose image is infinite. So x \in K \iff p_x \in L, and since K \notin \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}, also L \notin \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}.




B. L \in \mathbf{R}


L is not decidable. By Rice’s theorem, “the image of \varphi_p is finite” is a nontrivial semantic property, so L \notin \mathbf{R}. In fact, L is not even in \mathbf{RE}\cup \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE} (see the correct answer).




C. L \in \mathbf{RE}\setminus \mathbf{R}


L is not in \mathbf{RE}, because \overline{K} \leqslant_m L. Given x, build a program q_x that, on input y, first runs M_x(x) and then outputs y. If M_x(x)\downarrow, then q_x computes the identity, whose image is infinite. If M_x(x)\uparrow, then q_x never outputs anything, so its image is empty, and hence finite. So x \in \overline{K} \iff q_x \in L, and since \overline{K} \notin \mathbf{RE}, also L \notin \mathbf{RE}.




D. L \notin \mathbf{RE}\cup \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}


We give two reductions.

\overline{K} \leqslant_m L: map x to a program that runs M_x(x) and then outputs its input y. Its image is empty if M_x(x)\uparrow and infinite if M_x(x)\downarrow. Hence L \notin \mathbf{RE}.
K \leqslant_m L: map x to a program that, on input y, outputs 1 if M_x(x) halts within |y| steps, and outputs y otherwise. Its image is finite if M_x(x)\downarrow and infinite if M_x(x)\uparrow. Hence L \notin \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}.

So L is neither in \mathbf{RE} nor in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}.





Exercise 28.7 (Many-one reductions and complexity classes (Partial exam 2, 05/06/2026))  

Which of the following statements is correct?
Recall that \mathbf{P} is the class of languages decidable in polynomial time, and that A \leqslant_m B means that there is a many-one reduction from A to B, not necessarily computable in polynomial time.




A. If B \in \mathbf{P} and A \leqslant_m B, then A \in \mathbf{P}.


This statement is false, because the reduction may take much more than polynomial time. Take any language A \in \mathbf{EXP}\setminus \mathbf{P}, which exists by the time hierarchy theorem, and let B = \{1\}. The reduction decides A by itself, in exponential time, and outputs 1 if w \in A and 0 otherwise. So A \leqslant_m B and B \in \mathbf{P}, but A \notin \mathbf{P}. This property only holds for polynomial-time reductions.




B. If A \in \mathbf{R}, there is a language B \in \mathbf{P} such that A \leqslant_m B.


This statement is true. Take B = \{1\}, which is in \mathbf{P}. The reduction f decides A, which is possible because A \in \mathbf{R}, and outputs f(w) = 1 if w \in A and f(w) = 0 otherwise. Then w \in A \iff f(w) \in B, and f is computable (although perhaps very slowly). So, without a time bound on the reduction, every decidable language reduces to a trivial language in \mathbf{P}.




C. If B \in \mathbf{P} and A \leqslant_m B, then A might not belong to \mathbf{R}.


This statement is false. If A \leqslant_m B and B \in \mathbf{R}, then A \in \mathbf{R}: to decide whether w \in A, compute f(w) and decide whether f(w) \in B. Since \mathbf{P}\subseteq \mathbf{R}, every language that reduces to a language in \mathbf{P} is decidable. Equivalently, if A \notin \mathbf{R} and A \leqslant_m B, then B \notin \mathbf{R}.




D. If B \in \mathbf{NP} and A \leqslant_m B, then A \in \mathbf{NP}.


This statement is false, for the same reason as the first option. By the time hierarchy theorem, there is a decidable language A that is not in \mathbf{EXP}, for example one decidable in doubly exponential time. Since \mathbf{NP}\subseteq \mathbf{EXP}, A \notin \mathbf{NP}. But A \leqslant_m \{1\} by the reduction that decides A and outputs 1 or 0, and \{1\} \in \mathbf{P}\subseteq \mathbf{NP}. Closure of \mathbf{NP} under reductions only holds for polynomial-time reductions.

title: Topics in Complexity
text:
Goals
In this part of the course we focus on computational complexity. We group languages into complexity classes by the resources (time, space, randomness, …) needed to decide them. We no longer ask whether a problem can be solved at all, but we focus on how much time a Turing machine needs to solve it, mainly we focus on the classes \mathbf{P}, \mathbf{NP}, \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP} and \mathbf{EXP}.
The central open question is whether \mathbf{P}\stackrel{?}{=} \mathbf{NP}. In this part of the course we study how to compare the difficulty of problems using polynomial-time reductions, why \mathtt{SAT} plays a special role, and what we can (and cannot) prove about how the complexity classes relate to each other.
At the end of this part of the course you should be able to:

title: 29  Decision, search and optimization problems
text:
29.1 Why we focus on decision problems
We use a CNF formula F to illustrate three possible different type of natural questions we can ask about computational problems: decision, search, and optimization. Very likely you have already seen the definition of formulas in Conjuntive Normal Form (CNF), if not look at the beginning of Chapter 33.
Click on the panels below to expand on each of them.
In complexity theory we almost always work with decision problems. There are several reasons for this.
They are languages. A decision problem is a language, and a TM that solves it simply accepts or rejects, exactly as in the computability part of the course. So we can keep using the same model, and complexity classes such as \mathbf{P} and \mathbf{NP} are simply sets of languages. There is no need to say what it means for a TM to “output” an assignment or a tour, or to compare the quality of outputs.
Reductions are simpler. A many-one reduction L_1 \leqslant_p L_2 only has to map yes-instances to yes-instances and no-instances to no-instances. Reductions between search or optimization problems also have to translate solutions back, which makes them more cumbersome to define and to use.
Hardness transfers upwards. A decision problem is never harder than its search or optimization versions. If we can find a satisfying assignment, we can certainly tell whether one exists. If we can find a largest clique, we can tell whether there is a clique of size k. So if the decision version is hard, the other versions are hard too. Since lower bounds are what we are after (for example, showing that \mathtt{SAT}\notin \mathbf{P}), nothing is lost by proving them for the decision version.
Usually, nothing is lost at all. For many natural problems, the converse also holds: a polynomial-time algorithm for the decision version gives a polynomial-time algorithm for the search and optimization versions.
So, for problems like \mathtt{SAT}, \mathtt{CLIQUE} or \mathtt{TSP}, the three versions are either all solvable in polynomial time or none of them is. The decision version captures the difficulty of the problem.
crumbs: 29  Decision, search and optimization problems

title: 29  Decision, search and optimization problems
text:
From optimization to decision: to compute the optimal value, run binary search over the threshold k. The optimum is at most 2^{p(|w|)} for some polynomial p, so only \mathcal{O}(p(|w|)) calls to the decision algorithm are needed.
From search to decision: many problems in \mathbf{NP} are self-reducible, meaning that we can build a solution one piece at a time by asking decision questions. Exercise 33.4 shows how to do this for \mathtt{SAT}.








WarningCaution



Search can be harder than decision when the decision question doesn’t really ask about the solutions. A standard example is factoring. Deciding whether n is composite is in \mathbf{P} (by the AKS primality test, 2002), but no polynomial-time algorithm is known for finding a nontrivial factor of n on a classical computer. Here the decision algorithm tells us that a factor exists without giving us any information about what it is. The security of RSA cryptosystem depends on this gap.
On a quantum computer, the situation is different: Shor’s algorithm (1994) factors integers in polynomial time. Quantum computers large enough to break RSA in practice do not exist yet, but this has motivated post-quantum cryptography, which builds cryptosystems on problems that are believed to be hard even for quantum computers, such as problems on lattices. In 2024, NIST standardized the first such schemes (ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA), and they are now being deployed to replace RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography.

title: 30  \mathbf{P}\subsetneq \mathbf{EXP}
text:
30.1 \mathbf{P} and \mathbf{EXP}
In this chapter we focus on how much time Turing machines need to solve problems. Intuitively, with more time, a Turing machine should be able to decide more languages. This section is about making this intuition precise.
Throughout this chapter, Turing machines are multitape.
The constant c is chosen together with M, and it is the same for all inputs: it may depend on L, but not on w. Equivalently, L \in \mathbf{TIME}(t(n)) if and only if L is decided by a TM whose running time is \mathcal{O}(t(n)). The constant c makes the definition independent of small details of the machine, such as its tape alphabet. A TM can always be sped up by a constant factor by working with larger tape symbols, each of which encodes several of the old ones.
\mathbf{P} is the standard formalization of “efficiently solvable” (the Cobham–Edmonds thesis). This choice has two good features. First, \mathbf{P} does not depend on the details of the model: single-tape and multitape TMs, RAM machines and all other reasonable deterministic models simulate each other with only a polynomial slowdown. Second, \mathbf{P} is closed under composition, since running one polynomial-time algorithm on the output of another takes polynomial time. In practice, polynomial-time algorithms almost always have small exponents.
The proof of \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{EXP} is a diagonalization argument, the same idea as the proof that \mathtt{K} is undecidable (Theorem 26.2). We build a machine D that, on input x, simulates the machine encoded by x and does the opposite. To make this work with time bounds, we need two ingredients:

title: 30  \mathbf{P}\subsetneq \mathbf{EXP}
text:
Definition 30.2 (\mathbf{P} and \mathbf{EXP}) 
\mathbf{P}= \bigcup_{k \geqslant 1} \mathbf{TIME}(n^k), \qquad \mathbf{EXP}= \bigcup_{k \geqslant 1} \mathbf{TIME}(2^{n^k}).




Exercise 30.1 (🌱) \mathbf{P}\subseteq \mathbf{EXP}.



D must be able to compute its own time budget, which leads to time-constructible functions;
we need to know how much it costs to simulate one machine with another.


30.1.1 The cost of universal simulation
Recall that a universal TM U, given \langle M, w \rangle, simulates M on w. We now also care about its speed. U has fixed alphabets and a fixed number of tapes, but M can have arbitrarily many states, tape symbols and tapes. So each step of M costs U several steps: it has to look up the transition of M in the encoding \langle M \rangle, and to manage the tapes of M with its own fixed number of tapes.

Theorem 30.1 (Universal simulation) There is a universal TM U such that, for every TM M, there is a constant c_M with the following property. For every input w, if M halts on w within t steps, then U on \langle M, w \rangle halts within c_M \cdot t^2 steps with the same answer.






NoteProof (sketch)





We assume t \geqslant|w|, as is always the case for the time bounds we use (a machine that runs in time less than |w| cannot read its whole input). Let M have states Q, tape alphabet \Gamma and k tapes. U has a fixed number of tapes, say four:

an input tape, containing \langle M, w \rangle;
a description tape, holding a copy of \langle M \rangle, the transition table of M;
a state tape, holding the current state of M, written in binary with \lceil \log |Q| \rceil bits;
a work tape, on which U stores all k tapes of M at once.

The key point is that U has a fixed alphabet and a fixed number of states, while M can have arbitrarily many symbols, states and tapes. So U cannot remember a symbol or a state of M in its own finite control. It must write them down and compare them bit by bit. All such costs depend only on M, and they are absorbed into the constant c_M.
Representing the tapes of M. Each symbol of \Gamma is written in binary with b = \lceil \log |\Gamma| \rceil bits. The work tape of U is divided into blocks. Block i stores cell i of each of the k tapes of M, together with one extra bit per tape marking whether the head of that tape is on cell i: 
\underbrace{\ a_1\, h_1\ \ a_2\, h_2\ \ \cdots\ \ a_k\, h_k\ }_{\text{block } i}, \qquad a_j \in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}^b,\ h_j \in \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}.
 Each block has length B = k(b+1), which depends only on M. So the k tapes of M become k “tracks” of a single tape. At the start, U copies w into the first track, in this format, in \mathcal{O}(B \cdot |w|) steps.
Simulating one step of M. Suppose the tapes of M use \ell cells so far, so that the work tape of U uses B\ell cells.

Collect. Sweep the work tape from left to right. Whenever a head bit h_j = \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}} is found, copy the symbol a_j to a scratch area. This gives the k symbols currently under the heads of M. Cost: \mathcal{O}(B\ell).
Look up. Search the description tape for the transition whose state matches the state tape and whose symbols match the scratch area. Cost: \mathcal{O}(|\langle M \rangle|^2), which is a constant depending only on M.
Update. Write the new state on the state tape. Sweep the work tape again, and at each head position write the new symbol and move the head bit to the neighbouring block, to the left or to the right. Cost: \mathcal{O}(B\ell).

So one simulated step costs at most c'_M \cdot \ell steps of U, for a constant c'_M depending only on M.
Total time. In each step, a head of M moves at most one cell, so after s steps the tapes of M use at most \ell \leqslant|w| + s + 1 \leqslant 2t + 1 cells. Hence simulating t steps of M costs at most 
\mathcal{O}(B|w|) + \sum_{s=1}^{t} c'_M\, (2t+1) \;\leqslant\; c_M \cdot t^2
 steps of U, for a suitable constant c_M. When M halts, U reads the state tape and gives the same answer.




The constant c_M depends on M, through its number of states, tapes and tape symbols, but not on w or t. The square comes from simulating the many tapes of M on the fixed number of tapes of U: each simulated step may require a sweep over the part of the tape used so far, which has length at most t. Better simulations exist, with a slowdown of only c_M\, t \log t, but t^2 is enough for our purposes. 
The constant c_M causes a problem for diagonalization. When D simulates M on input x = \langle M \rangle, the simulation costs about c_M \cdot t^2 steps, and for a short encoding x, this may be more than the budget of D allows. The solution is to make sure that every machine has encodings that are as long as we want.
We fix an encoding in which every TM has infinitely many encodings. For example, we let any word of the form \langle M \rangle\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\$}}\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^j, for j \geqslant 0, encode M. Then M has encodings of every sufficiently large length. On a long enough encoding of M, the budget of D grows faster than c_M, so the simulation always finishes in time.
From now on, for a word x, we write M_x for the machine encoded by x. If x is not a valid encoding, M_x is a fixed machine that rejects every input.


30.1.2 Time hierarchy theorem (special case) and \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{EXP}

Theorem 30.2 (Time hierarchy theorem (special case)) 
\mathbf{TIME}(2^n) \subsetneq \mathbf{TIME}(2^{n^2}).







NoteProof





Clearly \mathbf{TIME}(2^n) \subseteq \mathbf{TIME}(2^{n^2}). We construct a language in \mathbf{TIME}(2^{n^2}) that is not in \mathbf{TIME}(2^n). Consider the following TM D:

On input x, with |x| = n:

Write \mathrm{bin}(2^{n^2}), that is, a \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}} followed by n^2 zeros, on a separate tape. This takes \mathcal{O}(n^2) steps, and the number will serve as a clock.
Using U, simulate M_x on input x. After each step of D, decrease the clock by one. If the clock reaches 0 before the simulation ends, stop and reject.
If the simulation ends before the clock reaches 0, do the opposite of M_x: accept if M_x rejected x, and reject if M_x accepted.


Decreasing a binary counter costs \mathcal{O}(1) steps on average, so D always halts within \mathcal{O}(2^{n^2}) steps. Hence \mathscr{L}(D) \in \mathbf{TIME}(2^{n^2}).
Suppose, for a contradiction, that \mathscr{L}(D) \in \mathbf{TIME}(2^n). Then some TM M decides \mathscr{L}(D) within c \cdot 2^n steps on inputs of length n, for some constant c. By Theorem 30.1, simulating M on an input of length n takes at most 
c_M \cdot (c \cdot 2^n)^2 = c_M c^2 \cdot 2^{2n}
 steps of D. Since 2^{2n} is less than 2^{n^2} for every n larger than some n_0, and M has encodings of every sufficiently large length, there is a word x with M_x = M and |x| > n_0. On this x, the simulation in step 2 finishes before the clock runs out, so in step 3, D gives the opposite answer of M on x. But M decides \mathscr{L}(D), so it gives the same answer as D on x. This is a contradiction. Hence \mathscr{L}(D) \notin \mathbf{TIME}(2^n).










Figure 30.1: The diagonalization in the proof of the time hierarchy theorem. Row M_{x_i} shows the answers of the machine encoded by x_i, run with the time budget of D. D disagrees with every machine on that machine’s own encoding. Since every machine that runs in time \mathcal{O}(2^n) has long encodings on which the simulation finishes in time, none of them decides \mathscr{L}(D).



This is a diagonalization argument, the same idea as Cantor’s proof that \mathbb{R} is uncountable (Theorem 3.1) and the proof that \mathtt{K} is undecidable (Theorem 26.2). See Figure 30.1. The machine D differs from every fast machine on at least one input, namely a long enough encoding of that machine. The new ingredient is the clock. In the proof that \mathtt{K} is undecidable, D might wait forever. Here, it cuts off every simulation at time 2^{n^2}, which guarantees that D itself runs in time \mathcal{O}(2^{n^2}).

Theorem 30.3 \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{EXP}






NoteProof





Every polynomial is eventually smaller than 2^n, so \mathbf{TIME}(n^k) \subseteq \mathbf{TIME}(2^n) for every k, and hence \mathbf{P}\subseteq \mathbf{TIME}(2^n). By the time hierarchy theorem (Theorem 30.2), 
\mathbf{P}\subseteq \mathbf{TIME}(2^n) \subsetneq \mathbf{TIME}(2^{n^2}) \subseteq \mathbf{EXP}.
 Hence \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{EXP}.




As it should be clear, the result from Theorem 30.2 can be strengthened by a more careful analysis. In particular, in the proof of Theorem 30.2 there is one subtle point, in step 1, we wanted to compute \mathrm{bin}(2^{n^2}) to use it as a clock, to do so, we need to compute \mathrm{bin}(2^{n^2}) in time less than \mathcal{O}(2^{n^2}). Which in this case is obvious, we used time \mathcal{O}(n^2). But for a generic function is not.

title: 30  \mathbf{P}\subsetneq \mathbf{EXP}
section: 30.2 Time constructible functions and the time hierarchy theorem
text:
30.2 Time constructible functions and the time hierarchy theorem
There are total computable functions f s.t. \mathbf{TIME}(f(n))= \mathbf{TIME}(2^{f(n)}), that is even if you are given exponentially more time, you cannot decide any new language. Such functions are pathological examples, and the problem arises when computing f(n) to allow a TM to take much more time than f(n). Avoiding such pathological examples gives rise to the notion of time-constructible functions.

Definition 30.3 (Time-constructible function) A function f\colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} is time-constructible if f(n) \geqslant n for all n, and there is a TM that, on input \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^n, writes \mathrm{bin}(f(n)) on its tape and halts within \mathcal{O}(f(n)) steps.

Essentially every function we would use as a time bound is time-constructible. In particular, n, n \log n, n^2, n^k, 2^n, 2^{n^k} and n! are all time-constructible. For example, to compute \mathrm{bin}(n^2) from \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^n, we count the input in binary, which takes \mathcal{O}(n) steps, and multiply in time \mathcal{O}(\log^2 n).
Moreover, if f(n) and g(n) are time-constructible, so are f(n) + g(n), f(n) \cdot g(n), f(g(n)) and 2^{f(n)}.
A notable function which is not time-constructible is \log n, because it is smaller than n, and a machine cannot even read its input in that time. Neither is any function that is not computable. A less obvious example is 
f(n) = \begin{cases} n^2 & \text{if the } n\text{-th TM halts on the empty input,} \\ n^3 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}

This function is perfectly reasonable as a time bound, but computing it would mean solving the halting problem.
This gives the following result.

Theorem 30.4 (Time hierarchy theorem (Hartmanis–Stearns, 1965)) Let g\colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} be time-constructible, and let f\colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} satisfy f(n) \log f(n) = o\big(g(n)\big). Then 
\mathbf{TIME}(f(n)) \subsetneq \mathbf{TIME}(g(n)).


This theorem has a lot of important consequences:

A hierarchy inside \mathbf{P}. For every k \geqslant 1, \mathbf{TIME}(n^k) \subsetneq \mathbf{TIME}(n^{k+1}), since n^k \log n^k = o(n^{k+1}). So some problems can be solved in time n^{100} but not in time n^{99}, and \mathbf{P} has no hardest level.
Finer gaps. \mathbf{TIME}(n) \subsetneq \mathbf{TIME}(n \log^2 n) and \mathbf{TIME}(n^2) \subsetneq \mathbf{TIME}(n^{2.01}).
Above \mathbf{EXP}. In the same way, \mathbf{EXP}\subsetneq 2\mathbf{EXP}= \bigcup_k \mathbf{TIME}(2^{2^{n^k}}), and so on. There is an infinite hierarchy of ever larger exponential classes.

title: 31  \mathbf{NP} and \mathbf{PH}
text:
31.1 The polynomial hierarchy
A deterministic TM has exactly one possible move in each configuration. A nondeterministic Turing machine (NTM) can have several. Its transition function has the form 
\delta\colon Q \times \Gamma \to \mathcal{P}(Q \times \Gamma \times \{L, R\}),
 so in each configuration the machine may choose among finitely many moves. On an input w, the possible computations of an NTM form a computation tree. The root is the start configuration, the children of a configuration are the configurations reachable from it in one step, and every path from the root is one possible computation (Figure 31.1). The NTM accepts w if at least one path reaches the accepting state.
We can think of an NTM as a machine that guesses well: if some sequence of choices leads to acceptance, the machine finds it. This is not a realistic model of computation, but it captures exactly the problems whose solutions are easy to check.
We have two equivalent ways of looking at \mathbf{NP}.
The second definition avoids nondeterminism. It only asks that membership be easy to check, given the right extra information.
The definition is asymmetric. If w \in L, some short certificate convinces V. If w \notin L, no certificate does, so V cannot be fooled.
We do not know whether either inclusion is strict. The question \mathbf{P}\stackrel{?}{=} \mathbf{NP} is the subject of the next chapter. We saw, however, that \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{EXP} (by the time hierarchy theorem), so at least one of the two inclusions in the previous theorem is strict.
\mathbf{P} is closed under complement: swap the accepting and rejecting states of the decider. For \mathbf{NP}, swapping does not work. The complement would have to reject when some computation accepts, that is, accept only when all computations reject. For example, a short certificate that F is satisfiable is easy to give, but there is no obvious short certificate that F is unsatisfiable. The class of complements of languages in \mathbf{NP} is called \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}, and whether \mathbf{NP}= \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP} is another open problem.
The polynomial hierarchy is the polynomial-time version of the arithmetic hierarchy we met in computability. Recall that a language L is in \mathbf{RE} if and only if there is a decidable relation R such that 
w \in L \iff \exists c\ \big[\, R(w, c) \,\big].
 Here c can be taken to be an accepting computation of a TM on w, and R checks that it is one. In the same way, L \in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE} if and only if w \in L \iff \forall c\ [\, R(w,c) \,]. Allowing more alternating quantifiers gives the arithmetic hierarchy, with levels \Sigma_n^0 and \Pi_n^0. So \Sigma_1^0 = \mathbf{RE}, \Pi_1^0 = \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}, and a language is in \Sigma_2^0 if it can be written as \exists c_1\, \forall c_2\, [\, R(w, c_1, c_2) \,], and so on.
\mathbf{NP} is defined in exactly the same way, with two changes: the relation must be checkable in polynomial time, and the certificates must be short. By definition, L is in \mathbf{NP} if there are a polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that 
w \in L \iff \exists c\ \big[\, |c| \leqslant p(|w|) \text{ and } V \text{ accepts } \langle w, c \rangle \,\big].
 So \mathbf{NP} consists of the languages defined by a single existential quantifier over short certificates, followed by a polynomial-time check. It is the polynomial-time analogue of \mathbf{RE}. Likewise, \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP} is the analogue of \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}: it consists of the languages defined by a single universal quantifier, 
w \in L \iff \forall c\ \big[\, |c| \leqslant p(|w|) \Rightarrow V \text{ accepts } \langle w, c \rangle \,\big].
 For example, F is unsatisfiable if and only if every assignment falsifies it. The polynomial hierarchy is what we get, as in the arithmetic hierarchy, by allowing several quantifiers alternating between \exists and \forall. This is why its levels are written \Sigma_k^p and \Pi_k^p. The superscript p stands for “polynomial”, just as the superscript 0 in \Sigma_n^0 indicates that the quantifiers range over finite objects such as words or numbers.
(*) In the arithmetic hierarchy, the decidable languages form the level \Delta_1^0 = \Sigma_1^0 \cap \Pi_1^0, because the “no quantifier” level contains only the decidable relations.
The analogy has limits, and they show what makes complexity theory harder. In computability, \mathbf{R}= \mathbf{RE}\cap \mathbf{co}\mathbf{RE}, and every level of the arithmetic hierarchy is known to be strictly contained in the next. In complexity, it is open whether \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}\cap \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}, and it is believed to be false: factoring is a candidate counterexample. It is not even known whether \Sigma_1^p \neq \Sigma_2^p, since that would imply \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}.
Many natural questions need more than one quantifier. Take the question “is there a formula with at most k symbols that is equivalent to F?” Equivalence is itself a \forall statement, so this question has the form 
\exists F' \ \forall \alpha \ \big[\, F' \text{ is a formula with }|F'| \leqslant k \text{ and $\alpha$ is an assignment s.t. } F'(\alpha) = F(\alpha) \,\big].
 It is not clear how to express it with a single quantifier.
To keep the notation short, we write \exists^p c for “there is a c with |c| \leqslant p(|w|)”, and \forall^p c for “for every c with |c| \leqslant p(|w|)”.
In particular, \Sigma_1^p = \mathbf{NP} and \Pi_1^p = \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}. Negating a formula with alternating quantifiers swaps \exists and \forall, and the negation of “V accepts” is “V rejects”, which can also be checked in polynomial time. So 
\Pi_k^p = \mathbf{co}\Sigma_k^p = \{\, \overline{L} : L \in \Sigma_k^p \,\}.
The known inclusions are summarized in Figure 31.2. As with \mathbf{P}\stackrel{?}{=} \mathbf{NP}, we do not know whether any of them is strict.
It is widely believed that the hierarchy is infinite, that is, \Sigma_k^p \subsetneq \Sigma_{k+1}^p for every k. If one level is closed under complement, then the hierarchy stops growing at that level. We prove the case k = 0.
The same argument, merging two adjacent quantifiers of the same kind into one, gives the general statement.
These results are often used as evidence. A statement that would make \mathbf{PH} collapse is considered very unlikely, almost as unlikely as \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}. For example, if graph isomorphism were \mathbf{NP}-complete, then \mathbf{PH} would collapse to \Sigma_2^p. This is the main reason it is believed not to be \mathbf{NP}-complete.
