Definition 31.4 (The polynomial hierarchy) Let k \geqslant 1. A language L is in \Sigma_k^p if there are a polynomial-time TM V and a polynomial p such that, for every w, 
w \in L \iff \exists^p c_1\ \forall^p c_2\ \exists^p c_3 \cdots Q_k c_k\ \ V \text{ accepts } \langle w, c_1, \dots, c_k \rangle,
 where the quantifiers alternate and Q_k is \exists if k is odd and \forall if k is even. A language is in \Pi_k^p if the same holds with the quantifiers starting with \forall: 
w \in L \iff \forall^p c_1\ \exists^p c_2\ \forall^p c_3 \cdots Q_k c_k\ \ V \text{ accepts } \langle w, c_1, \dots, c_k \rangle.
 We set \Sigma_0^p = \Pi_0^p = \mathbf{P}, and define the polynomial hierarchy as 
\mathbf{PH}= \bigcup_{k \geqslant 0} \Sigma_k^p.





Theorem 31.3 For every k \geqslant 0:

\Sigma_k^p \cup \Pi_k^p \subseteq \Sigma_{k+1}^p \cap \Pi_{k+1}^p.
\mathbf{PH}\subseteq \mathbf{EXP}.







NoteProof






A verifier can ignore some of its certificates. If L \in \Sigma_k^p, we can add an unused quantifier at the end, which shows L \in \Sigma_{k+1}^p, or at the beginning, which shows L \in \Pi_{k+1}^p. The same argument works for \Pi_k^p.
Let L \in \Sigma_k^p, with verifier V and polynomial p. A deterministic TM can evaluate the quantifiers by brute force. It loops over all c_1 with |c_1| \leqslant p(n), inside that over all c_2, and so on, runs V on each tuple, and combines the answers with “or” for \exists and “and” for \forall. There are at most 2^{O(k\, p(n))} tuples, each checked in polynomial time. Since k is a constant, this takes time 2^{O(p(n))}, so L \in \mathbf{EXP}.












Figure 31.2: The polynomial hierarchy. All the inclusions shown are known; none of them is known to be strict.





Theorem 31.4 If \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}, then \mathbf{PH}= \mathbf{P}.






NoteProof





We show \Sigma_k^p = \Pi_k^p = \mathbf{P} by induction on k. The case k = 0 holds by definition. Suppose \Sigma_k^p = \Pi_k^p = \mathbf{P}, and let L \in \Sigma_{k+1}^p: 
w \in L \iff \exists^p c_1\ \underbrace{\forall^p c_2 \cdots Q_{k+1} c_{k+1}\ \ V \text{ accepts } \langle w, c_1, \dots, c_{k+1} \rangle}_{\text{this says } \langle w, c_1 \rangle \in L'}.
 The language L' is defined by k alternating quantifiers starting with \forall, so L' \in \Pi_k^p = \mathbf{P}. The bounds |c_i| \leqslant p(|w|) are still polynomial in |\langle w, c_1 \rangle|. So L is defined by a single \exists^p followed by a polynomial-time check, which means L \in \mathbf{NP}= \mathbf{P}. Hence \Sigma_{k+1}^p = \mathbf{P}, and \Pi_{k+1}^p = \mathbf{co}\mathbf{P}= \mathbf{P}.






Exercise 31.2 If \Sigma_k^p = \Pi_k^p for some k \geqslant 1, then \mathbf{PH}= \Sigma_k^p. In particular, if \mathbf{NP}= \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}, then \mathbf{PH}= \mathbf{NP}.

title: 32  \mathbf{P} vs \mathbf{NP}
text:
32.1 \mathbf{P}\stackrel{?}{=}\mathbf{NP} and Impagliazzo’s five worlds
In this chapter we introduce polynomial-time reductions and \mathbf{NP}-completeness, the tools we use to compare the difficulty of problems in \mathbf{NP}. We start with the question that motivates the whole theory, whether \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}, and with Impagliazzo’s description of what the world would look like under different answers. We then show that, if \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}, there are problems in \mathbf{NP} that are neither easy nor \mathbf{NP}-complete (Ladner’s theorem). Finally, we explain why the diagonalization and simulation techniques from computability cannot settle the question (relativization).
We know that \mathbf{P}\subseteq \mathbf{NP}: a polynomial-time decider is a verifier that ignores its certificate. Whether the inclusion is strict is the most famous open problem in theoretical computer science, and one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems of the Clay Mathematics Institute.
Informally, the question is: if a solution can be checked quickly, can it also be found quickly? Most researchers believe the answer is no, so that \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}. One reason is the lack of progress: decades of work on \mathbf{NP}-complete problems in many different areas have never produced a polynomial-time algorithm for any of them. Another is that \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP} would make many tasks that seem to need creativity, such as finding a proof of a theorem whose proof is short, as easy as checking a solution.
There is also a third possibility: that the question has no answer in our usual axioms. Like the continuum hypothesis, the statement \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP} might be independent of \mathsf{ZFC}, meaning that it can be neither proved nor disproved from the standard axioms of set theory. Some partial results point in this direction. For example, Hartmanis and Hopcroft (1976) constructed oracles A for which the question “\mathbf{P}^A \stackrel{?}{=} \mathbf{NP}^A” is independent of \mathsf{ZFC} (we will see oracles at the end of this chapter). However, there is no evidence that the unrelativized question is independent, and most researchers expect it to be settled by an ordinary proof. Proving that it is independent would itself require techniques far beyond what we currently have.
\mathbf{P} versus \mathbf{NP} is a question about the worst case, and the two possible answers do not tell the whole story. In 1995, Russell Impagliazzo described five possible “worlds”, depending on how hard \mathbf{NP} is on average, and on whether cryptography is possible:
The five worlds are listed from “most algorithms” to “most cryptography”. We do not know which one we live in. Even proving \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP} would only rule out Algorithmica.

title: 32  \mathbf{P} vs \mathbf{NP}
text:
World
What holds
Consequences




Algorithmica
\mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}, or \mathbf{NP} is easy in some practical sense.
Search and optimization problems in \mathbf{NP} become easy, and so does finding short proofs. Essentially no cryptography is possible.


Heuristica
\mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}, but \mathbf{NP} problems are easy on average.
Hard instances exist, but it is as hard to find them as to solve them. In practice, this looks almost like Algorithmica.


Pessiland
\mathbf{NP} is hard on average, but one-way functions do not exist.
The worst of both worlds: we can create hard problems, but we cannot use them to build cryptography.


Minicrypt
One-way functions exist, but public-key cryptography does not.
Private-key encryption, pseudorandom generators and digital signatures are possible, but parties who have never met cannot agree on a secret key.


Cryptomania
Public-key cryptography exists.
The world most researchers believe we live in, and the one modern cryptography relies on. Examples are RSA, which relies on factoring, and the post-quantum schemes based on lattices.

title: 32  \mathbf{P} vs \mathbf{NP}
text:
32.2 Poly-time reductions and \mathbf{NP}-completeness
To compare the difficulty of two problems, we use the polynomial-time version of the many-one reductions from computability.

Definition 32.1 (Polynomial-time reduction) Let L_1 \subseteq \Sigma_1^* and L_2 \subseteq \Sigma_2^*. A polynomial-time reduction from L_1 to L_2 is a function f\colon \Sigma_1^* \to \Sigma_2^*, computable in polynomial time, such that for every w \in \Sigma_1^*, 
w \in L_1 \iff f(w) \in L_2.
 If such an f exists, we write L_1 \leqslant_p L_2 and say that L_1 reduces to L_2.

We read L_1 \leqslant_p L_2 as “L_1 is not harder than L_2”: to decide L_1, translate the input with f and then decide L_2.

Lemma 32.1 Let L_1, L_2 and L_3 be languages.

If L_1 \leqslant_p L_2 and L_2 \leqslant_p L_3, then L_1 \leqslant_p L_3.
If L_1 \leqslant_p L_2 and L_2 \in \mathbf{P}, then L_1 \in \mathbf{P}.
If L_1 \leqslant_p L_2 and L_2 \in \mathbf{NP}, then L_1 \in \mathbf{NP}.







NoteProof





Let f be a reduction computable in time p(n), for some polynomial p. A TM can write at most one symbol per step, so |f(w)| \leqslant p(|w|). For 1., if g reduces L_2 to L_3 in time q(n), then g \circ f reduces L_1 to L_3 in time p(n) + q(p(n)), which is polynomial. For 2., to decide whether w \in L_1, compute f(w) and run a polynomial-time decider for L_2 on it. This takes time polynomial in |f(w)| \leqslant p(|w|), and hence in |w|. The proof of 3. is the same, using a verifier for L_2 instead of a decider.





Definition 32.2 (\mathbf{NP}-hard and \mathbf{NP}-complete) A language L is \mathbf{NP}-hard if L' \leqslant_p L for every L' \in \mathbf{NP}. It is \mathbf{NP}-complete if it is \mathbf{NP}-hard and L \in \mathbf{NP}.

The \mathbf{NP}-complete languages are the hardest languages in \mathbf{NP}. If any one of them can be decided in polynomial time, then all of \mathbf{NP} can.

Theorem 32.1 Let L be \mathbf{NP}-complete. Then L \in \mathbf{P} if and only if \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}.






NoteProof





If \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}, then L \in \mathbf{NP}= \mathbf{P}. Conversely, suppose L \in \mathbf{P}, and let L' \in \mathbf{NP}. Then L' \leqslant_p L, so L' \in \mathbf{P} by Lemma 32.1.




So, to prove \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}, it is enough to show that a single \mathbf{NP}-complete problem, such as \mathtt{SAT}, has no polynomial-time algorithm. The difficulty is to find a first \mathbf{NP}-complete problem. After that, transitivity does the rest.

Corollary 32.1 Let L_1 be \mathbf{NP}-complete, and let L_2 \in \mathbf{NP} be such that L_1 \leqslant_p L_2. Then L_2 is \mathbf{NP}-complete.






NoteProof





For every L \in \mathbf{NP}, we have L \leqslant_p L_1 \leqslant_p L_2, so L \leqslant_p L_2 by transitivity.




This gives the standard way to prove that a new language L is \mathbf{NP}-complete:

Show that L \in \mathbf{NP}, by giving a certificate and a polynomial-time verifier.
Choose a known \mathbf{NP}-complete language L', often 3\mathtt{SAT}.
Give a polynomial-time reduction f from L' to L. Note the direction: from the known problem to the new one.
Prove that w \in L' \Rightarrow f(w) \in L and that f(w) \in L \Rightarrow w \in L'. Proving only one direction is a common mistake.

The first \mathbf{NP}-complete language comes from the Cook–Levin theorem (Theorem 33.1), which shows that \mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete. Every other problem in Figure 32.1 is then shown to be \mathbf{NP}-complete by a chain of reductions starting from it. Since Cook (1971), Karp (1972) and Levin (1973), thousands of problems from logic, graph theory, scheduling, biology and many other areas have been shown to be \mathbf{NP}-complete in this way.






Figure 32.1: The \mathbf{NP}-complete problems in this course. An arrow A \to B means A \leqslant_p B.









TipRemark: other kinds of reductions



A many-one reduction calls the “algorithm” for L_2 only once, at the end, and must return its answer unchanged. A Turing reduction (also called a Cook reduction) may call it many times and process the answers. With Turing reductions, \mathtt{SAT} and its complement \overline{\mathtt{SAT}} reduce to each other. Many-one reductions are finer: they can tell \mathbf{NP} apart from \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}. For example, if an \mathbf{NP}-complete language were in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}, then \mathbf{NP}= \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}.

title: 32  \mathbf{P} vs \mathbf{NP}
text:
32.3 \mathbf{NP}-intermediate problems






Warning



This section contains parts that are more advanced. When you’ll get lost continue with the rest of the computability part of the course, and come back to this section on a second read.


If \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}, the picture is simple. Every language in \mathbf{P} other than \emptyset and \Sigma^* is \mathbf{NP}-complete, since a reduction can solve the instance itself and output a fixed yes-instance or a fixed no-instance. If \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}, then \mathbf{P} and the \mathbf{NP}-complete languages are disjoint subsets of \mathbf{NP}, and it is natural to ask whether together they cover all of \mathbf{NP} (Figure 32.2).

Definition 32.3 A language L is \mathbf{NP}-intermediate if L \in \mathbf{NP}, L \notin \mathbf{P}, and L is not \mathbf{NP}-complete.







Figure 32.2: The structure of \mathbf{NP} under the two possible answers to \mathbf{P}\stackrel{?}{=} \mathbf{NP}. Ladner’s theorem shows that, if \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}, the \mathbf{NP}-intermediate region is not empty.



Several natural problems are believed to be \mathbf{NP}-intermediate:

Factoring. The decision version \{\langle n, k \rangle : n \text{ has a factor } d \text{ with } 1 < d \leqslant k\} is in \mathbf{NP}\cap \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}. So it is not \mathbf{NP}-complete unless \mathbf{NP}= \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}, and no classical polynomial-time algorithm for it is known.
Graph isomorphism. Deciding whether two graphs are isomorphic is not \mathbf{NP}-complete unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses. In 2015, Babai gave an algorithm for it that runs in quasi-polynomial time, 2^{(\log n)^{O(1)}}, but no polynomial-time algorithm is known.
Discrete logarithm. It has a status similar to factoring, and is also used in cryptography.

None of these is proved to be \mathbf{NP}-intermediate. A proof would in particular show that \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}. What we can prove is that, if \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}, some \mathbf{NP}-intermediate language exists.

Theorem 32.2 (Ladner, 1975) If \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}, then there is a language L \in \mathbf{NP} that is \mathbf{NP}-intermediate: L \notin \mathbf{P}, and L is not \mathbf{NP}-complete.






NoteProof (Sketch)





The idea is to “blow holes” in \mathtt{SAT} by padding its instances. With little padding, the result is still as hard as \mathtt{SAT}. With a lot of padding, it becomes easy, because a polynomial in the padded length can be exponential in the original length. Ladner’s trick is to choose the amount of padding so that neither happens.
For a function H\colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}, let 
\mathtt{SAT}_H = \{\, \langle F \rangle\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\$}}\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^{n^{H(n)}} : \langle F \rangle \in \mathtt{SAT}\text{ and } n = |\langle F \rangle| \,\},
 where \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\$}} is a new symbol. Fix an enumeration M_1, M_2, \dots of all TMs in which every TM appears infinitely often, and define H(n) as follows:

H(n) is the smallest i < \log \log n such that, for every x with |x| \leqslant\log n, the machine M_i decides correctly whether x \in \mathtt{SAT}_H within i|x|^i steps. If there is no such i, then H(n) = \log \log n.

This definition is recursive: to decide whether x \in \mathtt{SAT}_H for |x| \leqslant\log n, we only need the values H(m) with m \leqslant\log n. One checks that H(n) can be computed in time polynomial in n. It follows that \mathtt{SAT}_H \in \mathbf{NP}: check that the padding has the right length, and guess a satisfying assignment of F.
Claim 1: if \mathtt{SAT}_H \in \mathbf{P}, then \mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P}. Suppose some TM M decides \mathtt{SAT}_H in time c n^c. Then M = M_i for some i \geqslant c. For all large n, the machine M_i passes the test in the definition, so H(n) \leqslant i. Hence H is bounded by a constant C. The map \langle F \rangle \mapsto \langle F \rangle\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\$}}\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^{n^{H(n)}} adds padding of length at most n^C, so it is a polynomial-time reduction from \mathtt{SAT} to \mathtt{SAT}_H. Therefore \mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P}.
Claim 2: if \mathtt{SAT}_H \notin \mathbf{P}, then H(n) \to \infty. Each M_i fails to decide \mathtt{SAT}_H within time i|x|^i on some input x. Once \log n \geqslant|x| (and \log \log n > i), we have H(n) \neq i. This holds for every i, so H(n) \to \infty.
Claim 3: if \mathtt{SAT}_H is \mathbf{NP}-complete, then \mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P}. Suppose f reduces \mathtt{SAT} to \mathtt{SAT}_H in time n^c, so |f(\langle F \rangle)| \leqslant n^c where n = |\langle F \rangle|. By Claim 1, we may assume \mathtt{SAT}_H \notin \mathbf{P}, since otherwise \mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P} already. So H(m) \to \infty by Claim 2, and H(m) > 2c for all m larger than some constant. If f(\langle F \rangle) does not have the form \langle F' \rangle\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\$}}\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}^{m^{H(m)}}, then F \notin \mathtt{SAT}. Otherwise m^{H(m)} \leqslant n^c, so for large m we get m \leqslant\sqrt{n}. Then F is satisfiable if and only if F' is, and F' is a formula of length at most \sqrt{n}. Repeating this, the length goes from n to \sqrt{n}, to n^{1/4}, and so on, and reaches a constant after \mathcal{O}(\log \log n) rounds. At that point, we solve the instance by brute force. This gives a polynomial-time algorithm for \mathtt{SAT}.
Conclusion. Assume \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}. Then \mathtt{SAT}\notin \mathbf{P}, so \mathtt{SAT}_H \notin \mathbf{P} by Claim 1, and \mathtt{SAT}_H is not \mathbf{NP}-complete by Claim 3. Since \mathtt{SAT}_H \in \mathbf{NP}, it is \mathbf{NP}-intermediate.




The language \mathtt{SAT}_H is very artificial. Whether there is a natural \mathbf{NP}-intermediate problem, assuming \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}, is still open.

title: 32  \mathbf{P} vs \mathbf{NP}
text:
32.4 Relativization
In computability, we proved that \mathtt{HALT} is undecidable by diagonalization. In complexity theory, we use the same technique to prove the time hierarchy theorem. It is natural to try it on \mathbf{P} versus \mathbf{NP}. This section explains why that cannot work.
An oracle Turing machine with oracle A \subseteq \Sigma^* is a TM with an extra tape, the oracle tape, and a special query state. When the machine enters the query state with a word y on the oracle tape, it learns in a single step whether y \in A. We write \mathbf{P}^A and \mathbf{NP}^A for the classes of languages decided by polynomial-time deterministic and nondeterministic oracle TMs with oracle A.
Diagonalization and simulation treat machines as black boxes: they run them, count their steps and flip their answers. All of this works just as well for oracle machines. Such arguments relativize: if they prove a statement about \mathbf{P} and \mathbf{NP}, the same argument proves it about \mathbf{P}^A and \mathbf{NP}^A for every oracle A. The next theorem shows that no relativizing argument can settle \mathbf{P} versus \mathbf{NP}.

Theorem 32.3 (Baker, Gill, Solovay, 1975) There are oracles A and B such that 
\mathbf{P}^A = \mathbf{NP}^A \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathbf{P}^B \neq \mathbf{NP}^B.







NoteProof (Sketch)





The oracle A. Let A = \{\langle M, x, 1^n \rangle : M \text{ accepts } x \text{ within } 2^n \text{ steps}\}. With a single query to A, a polynomial-time machine can answer any question that can be decided in exponential time, so \mathbf{EXP}\subseteq \mathbf{P}^A. Conversely, a polynomial-time nondeterministic machine with oracle A has at most 2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)} computation paths. Each of its queries has polynomial length, and can be answered by a simulation that takes time 2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}. So \mathbf{NP}^A \subseteq \mathbf{EXP}. Hence 
\mathbf{P}^A \subseteq \mathbf{NP}^A \subseteq \mathbf{EXP}\subseteq \mathbf{P}^A,
 and all of these classes are equal.
The oracle B. For any oracle B, let 
U_B = \{\, 1^n : B \text{ contains a word of length } n \,\}.
 Then U_B \in \mathbf{NP}^B: guess a word of length n and query B about it. We build B so that U_B \notin \mathbf{P}^B. Let M_1, M_2, \dots be an enumeration of deterministic oracle TMs, where M_i is stopped after n^i steps. We build B in stages. In stage i:

Choose n larger than the length of every word queried in earlier stages, and with 2^n > n^i.
Run M_i on 1^n. Whenever it queries a word whose membership in B is already decided, answer accordingly. Otherwise answer “no”, and decide that the word is not in B.
If M_i accepts, put no word of length n in B, so 1^n \notin U_B. If M_i rejects, put into B a word of length n that M_i did not query. Such a word exists, because M_i made at most n^i < 2^n queries. Then 1^n \in U_B.

In both cases, M_i gives the wrong answer about 1^n, and later stages do not change this, because they only use longer words. Every polynomial-time oracle machine appears in the enumeration with a large enough time bound n^i, so no polynomial-time machine with oracle B decides U_B. Hence U_B \in \mathbf{NP}^B \setminus \mathbf{P}^B.




So a proof that \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP} cannot relativize, since it would also show that \mathbf{P}^A \neq \mathbf{NP}^A. A proof that \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP} cannot relativize either, since it would show that \mathbf{P}^B = \mathbf{NP}^B. Any solution must use some property of computation that is lost when machines are given an oracle. Two other barriers of the same kind are known: natural proofs (Razborov and Rudich, 1994) and algebrization (Aaronson and Wigderson, 2008). Each of them rules out a large family of proof techniques, which helps explain why the problem is still open.

title: 33  \mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete
text:
33.1 Propositional formulas
In this chapter we introduce (recall?) what \mathtt{SAT} is, we prove that it is \mathbf{NP}-complete, and we show some variations of it that are also \mathbf{NP}-complete and others that are in \mathbf{P}.
We consider Boolean (i.e. 0/1-valued) variables x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots. A literal is a variable x_i or its negation \neg x_i. A clause is a disjunction (\lor) of one or more literals. A formula in conjunctive normal form (CNF) is a conjunction (\land) of one or more clauses: 
F = C_1 \wedge C_2 \wedge \dots \wedge C_m, \qquad C_j = (\ell_{j,1} \vee \ell_{j,2} \vee \dots \vee \ell_{j,k_j}).
To give F as input to a Turing machine, we write it as a word over the finite alphabet 
\Sigma_{\mathtt{SAT}} = \{\, \mathtt{x},\ \mathtt{0},\ \mathtt{1},\ \neg,\ \vee,\ \wedge,\ (,\ )\,\}.
 There are infinitely many variables, so a variable can’t be a single symbol. We write its index in binary instead. The encoding \langle\cdot\rangle is defined as follows:
An assignment is a map \alpha\colon \{x_1,\dots,x_n\} \to \{0,1\}.1 It satisfies F if every clause contains at least one true literal: either some x_i with \alpha(x_i) = 1 or some \neg x_i with \alpha(x_i) = 0. The formula F is satisfiable if some assignment satisfies it.

title: 33  \mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete
text:
\langle x_i \rangle = \mathtt{x}\,\mathrm{bin}(i), where \mathrm{bin}(i) \in \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}},\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}\}^* is i \geqslant 1 in binary;
\langle \neg x_i \rangle = \neg\,\langle x_i \rangle;
\langle C \rangle = (\,\langle \ell_1 \rangle \vee \langle \ell_2 \rangle \vee \dots \vee \langle \ell_k \rangle\,) for a clause C = \ell_1 \vee \dots \vee \ell_k;
\langle  F \rangle = \langle C_1 \rangle \wedge \langle C_2 \rangle \wedge \dots \wedge \langle C_m \rangle for a formula F = C_1 \wedge \dots \wedge C_m.


Example 33.1 The formula 
F = (x_1 \vee \neg x_2) \wedge (x_2 \vee x_3 \vee \neg x_1)
 is encoded as the word 
\langle  F \rangle = (\mathtt{x1} \vee \neg\mathtt{x10}) \wedge (\mathtt{x10} \vee \mathtt{x11} \vee \neg\mathtt{x1}).





Example 33.2 (Satisfiable or not?) For each of the following CNF formulas, decide whether it is satisfiable. If it is, give a satisfying assignment. If it is not, explain why no assignment satisfies it.

F_1 = (x_1 \lor \lnot x_2 \lor x_3) \land (\lnot x_1 \lor x_2) \land (\lnot x_2 \lor \lnot x_3) \land (\lnot x_1 \lor x_3)
F_2 = (x_1 \lor x_2) \land (\lnot x_1 \lor x_3) \land (\lnot x_2 \lor x_3) \land (\lnot x_3 \lor x_1) \land (\lnot x_3 \lor \lnot x_1)







TipHint





You can always check all 2^3 = 8 assignments, but it is quicker to reason with the short clauses. Read a clause (\lnot x \lor y) as the implication x \to y, and see what follows from setting a variable to 1 or to 0.









NoteSolution






Satisfiable. Suppose x_1 = 1. Then the clauses (\lnot x_1 \lor x_2) and (\lnot x_1 \lor x_3) force x_2 = x_3 = 1, but then (\lnot x_2 \lor \lnot x_3) is false. So x_1 = 0. The first clause then becomes (\lnot x_2 \lor x_3), and setting x_2 = 0 satisfies it. So x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = 0 satisfies F_1. The assignment x_1 = x_2 = 0, x_3 = 1 is the only other one that does.
Unsatisfiable. The clauses (\lnot x_3 \lor x_1) and (\lnot x_3 \lor \lnot x_1) say that x_3 \to x_1 and x_3 \to \lnot x_1, so every satisfying assignment must have x_3 = 0. Then (\lnot x_1 \lor x_3) forces x_1 = 0, and (\lnot x_2 \lor x_3) forces x_2 = 0. But then (x_1 \lor x_2) is false. Hence no assignment satisfies F_2.






Exercise 33.1 (\mathrm{PHP}^m_n) In this exercise we construct a propositional formula encoding the pigenhole principle (see Section 2.2.1). For n\in \mathbb{N}, let [n]=\{1,\dots,n\}. For each i\in [m] and j\in [n], let p_{i,j} be a Boolean variable. The intended meaning of p_{i,j} is that p_{i,j}=1 if and only if the pigeon i flies to hole j. Consider the following CNF formula: 
\mathrm{PHP}^m_n=\bigwedge_{i\in [m]}(p_{i,1}\lor \cdots\lor p_{i,n})\ \land\ \bigwedge_{j\in [n]}\bigwedge_{\substack{i,i'\in [m]\\ i\neq i'}} (\lnot p_{i,j}\lor \lnot p_{i',j})\ .
\tag{33.1}

Show that an assignment that satisfies p_{i,1}\lor \cdots\lor p_{i,n} also satisfies p_{i,1}+ \cdots+ p_{i,n}\geqslant 1 (and viceversa);
Show that an assignment that satisfies \bigwedge_{\substack{i,i'\in [m]\\ j\neq j'}} (\lnot p_{i,j}\lor \lnot p_{i',j}) also satisfies p_{1,j}+ \cdots+ p_{m,j}\leqslant 1 (and viceversa);
Show that \langle\mathrm{PHP}^m_n\rangle\in \mathtt{SAT} if and only if m\leqslant n.

title: 33  \mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete
text:
33.2 \mathtt{SAT}
In this section we recall more precisely what \mathtt{SAT} is and we prove that it is \mathbf{NP}-complete. This language will be our first \mathbf{NP}-complete language and via reductions will allow to show that many more languages are \mathbf{NP}-complete.

Definition 33.1 (\mathtt{SAT}) 
\mathtt{SAT}= \{\, \langle F \rangle \in \Sigma_{\mathtt{SAT}}^* :F \text{ is a CNF formula and }  F \text{ is satisfiable} \,\}.
 A word that is not the encoding of any CNF formula is not in \mathtt{SAT}.

We have the following observations, which are left as an exercise about how some details of the definition of \mathtt{SAT} do not actually matter.

Exercise 33.2 (The encoding does not matter much)  

The encoding \langle \cdot \rangle is short. Suppose F has n variables, m clauses and L literal occurrences in total. Show that each literal takes at most 2 + \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1 symbols, and there are fewer than L + 3m separator symbols. So |\langle F\rangle| = \mathcal{O}(L \log n).
Checking the syntax is easy. Show that the set of words that encode some CNF formula is a regular language. A TM can therefore reject badly formed inputs in linear time. (Hence difficulty of \mathtt{SAT} lies entirely in deciding satisfiability.)
The choice of encoding \langle \cdot \rangle does not matter. Any reasonable encoding gives a word whose length is polynomially related to the length of the one we used. For example, give an encoding writing indices in unary, and total length \mathcal{O}(Ln), or list the variable count and clause count first. (A TM can translate between these encodings in polynomial time, so membership of \mathtt{SAT} in \mathbf{P} or \mathbf{NP}, and its \mathbf{NP}-completeness, do not depend on the encoding we chose.)


A well-known property is that \mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{EXP}.

Exercise 33.3 (\mathtt{SAT} in exponential time) Let F be a CNF formula, let N = |\langle F\rangle| be the length of its encoding, and let n be the number of distinct variables that appear in F.

Describe a multitape Turing machine that decides \mathtt{SAT} in time \mathcal{O}(2^n \cdot N^2). Give a high-level description of its tapes and phases, and estimate the asymptotic cost of each phase.






TipHint





There are 2^n assignments to the variables of F. How long does it take to check whether a single assignment satisfies F? Keep the current assignment on a separate tape and treat it as a binary counter.



Show that n \leqslant N/3.
Conclude that \mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{TIME}(2^N), and therefore \mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{EXP}.



We do not know whether \mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P}. But we know that \mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete.

Theorem 33.1 (Cook-Levin) \mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete.






NoteProof (sketch)





We have to show that \mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{NP}, and that L \leqslant_p \mathtt{SAT} for every L \in \mathbf{NP}.
\mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{NP}. The certificate for \langle F \rangle is an assignment \alpha of its variables. Its length is at most |\langle F \rangle|, and a verifier can check in polynomial time that a satisfies every clause of F.
\mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-hard. Let L \in \mathbf{NP}. Then there is a single-tape nondeterministic TM M = (Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, q_{\text{acc}}, q_{\text{rej}}) that decides L in time p(n), for some polynomial p. We modify M so that it never stops: once it is in q_{\text{acc}} or q_{\text{rej}}, it stays in that state, does not move its head and does not change the tape. Then every computation of M can be extended to one that runs for exactly p(n) steps.
Let w = w_1 \cdots w_n be an input and let N = p(n). We construct, in polynomial time, a CNF formula F_w such that 
w \in L \iff F_w \text{ is satisfiable}.

The tableau. We write a configuration of M as a word over \Gamma \cup Q: the tape contents, with the state written just before the cell under the head. In N steps, M visits at most N+1 cells, so each configuration fits in a word of length N+2. A tableau for w is an (N+1) \times (N+4) table whose rows are configurations, padded with blanks \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\sqcup}} and with a symbol \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}} at each end:

row 0 is the start configuration \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}}\, q_0\, w_1 \cdots w_n \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\sqcup}} \cdots \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\sqcup \#}};
each row i+1 follows from row i by one step of M.

The tableau is accepting if some row contains q_{\text{acc}}. So w \in L if and only if there is an accepting tableau for w.
The variables. Let C = Q \cup \Gamma \cup \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}}\}. For each cell (i,j) and each symbol s \in C, we introduce a variable x_{i,j,s}, meaning that cell (i,j) contains s. We define 
F_w = F_{\text{cell}} \land F_{\text{start}} \land F_{\text{accept}} \land F_{\text{move}},
 where:

F_{\text{cell}} says that every cell contains exactly one symbol: 
F_{\text{cell}} = \bigwedge_{i,j} \Big[ \Big( \bigvee_{s \in C} x_{i,j,s} \Big) \land \bigwedge_{s \neq t} (\lnot x_{i,j,s} \lor \lnot x_{i,j,t}) \Big].

F_{\text{start}} says that row 0 is the start configuration. It is a conjunction of single-literal clauses: x_{0,0,\#} \land x_{0,1,q_0} \land x_{0,2,w_1} \land \cdots \land x_{0,N+3,\#}.
F_{\text{accept}} says that q_{\text{acc}} appears somewhere. It is a single clause: \bigvee_{i,j} x_{i,j,q_{\text{acc}}}.
F_{\text{move}} says that each row follows from the previous one by a step of M. This is the key part, explained next.

Windows. A window is a 2 \times 3 block of cells, with three cells (i, j-1), (i,j), (i,j+1) in row i and the three cells below them in row i+1. The head moves at most one cell per step, so the contents of a cell in row i+1 depend only on the three cells above it. We call a window legal if it is consistent with \delta. For example, if (q', b, R) \in \delta(q, a), then the window with top row x\; q\; a and bottom row x\; b\; q' is legal. The set W \subseteq C^6 of legal windows depends only on M, not on w.
One can then show the following:

If row 0 is the start configuration and every window of the tableau is legal, then every row i+1 is a configuration that follows from row i by one step of M.

So it is enough for F_{\text{move}} to say that every window is legal. We do this by forbidding each illegal window: 
F_{\text{move}} = \bigwedge_{i,j}\ \bigwedge_{(a_1,\dots,a_6) \notin W} \big( \lnot x_{i,j-1,a_1} \lor \lnot x_{i,j,a_2} \lor \lnot x_{i,j+1,a_3} \lor \lnot x_{i+1,j-1,a_4} \lor \lnot x_{i+1,j,a_5} \lor \lnot x_{i+1,j+1,a_6} \big).

Correctness. If w \in L, then M has an accepting computation on w. Extending it to N steps gives an accepting tableau, and setting x_{i,j,s} = 1 exactly when cell (i,j) contains s satisfies F_w. Conversely, suppose an assignment satisfies F_w. By F_{\text{cell}}, it describes a table with one symbol in each cell. By F_{\text{start}} and F_{\text{move}}, together with the claim above, the rows of the table form a computation of M on w. By F_{\text{accept}}, this computation reaches q_{\text{acc}}. Hence w \in L.
Size and running time. The tableau has (N+1)(N+4) = O(p(n)^2) cells. Each part of F_w contributes a number of clauses per cell that depends only on |C| and |W|, that is, only on M. With indices written in binary, |\langle F_w \rangle| = O(p(n)^2 \log p(n)). The formula can be written out with a few nested loops over i, j and the symbols, so the map w \mapsto \langle F_w \rangle is computable in polynomial time. Therefore L \leqslant_p \mathtt{SAT}.





Exercise 33.4 (Search to decision for \mathtt{SAT}) Assume that \mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P}. Show that there is a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a CNF formula F, either outputs a satisfying assignment of F or reports that F is unsatisfiable.






TipHint





Let x_1, \dots, x_n be the variables of F, and write F|_{x_1 = b} for the formula obtained by setting x_1 to b and simplifying. That is, delete the clauses that become true and delete the literals that become false. Then F is satisfiable if and only if F|_{x_1 = 0} or F|_{x_1 = 1} is satisfiable. Fix the variables one at a time, using the algorithm for \mathtt{SAT} to choose a value for each one. How many times do you call that algorithm? Be careful with clauses that become empty.





Exercise 33.5 (Optimization to decision for \mathsf{MAX}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}) Let \mathsf{MAX}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}= \{\, \langle F, k \rangle : \text{some assignment satisfies at least } k \text{ clauses of } F \,\}. Assume that \mathsf{MAX}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P}. Show that there is a polynomial-time algorithm that, given F, outputs an assignment satisfying the largest possible number of clauses of F.






TipHint





First compute the optimal number of satisfied clauses k^*. Note that 0 \leqslant k^* \leqslant m, where m is the number of clauses. Then fix the variables one at a time, as in Exercise 33.4, keeping the value of each variable only if k^* clauses can still be satisfied. This time, don’t delete the clauses that become true; keep track of how many there are.

title: 33  \mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete
text:
33.3 Variants of \mathtt{SAT} \mathbf{NP}-complete
In this section we collect some (somewhat guided) exercises about variations of \mathtt{SAT} which remain \mathbf{NP}-complete.

Exercise 33.6 (k\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}, k\geqslant 3) A CNF formula F is a k-CNF if each clause of F has at most k literals. The language k\text{-}\mathtt{SAT} is 
k\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}= \{\, \langle F \rangle \in \Sigma_{\mathtt{SAT}}^* :F \text{ is a $k$-CNF formula and }  F \text{ is satisfiable} \,\}.
 Show that k\text{-}\mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete for every k\geqslant 3.






TipHint





Prove that 3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{NP} and construct a polynomial-time reduction showing that \mathtt{SAT}\leqslant_p 3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}. For the reduction, let C = \ell_1 \lor \ell_2 \lor \cdots \lor \ell_k be a clause with k \geqslant 4 literals, and let 
\tilde C = (\ell_1 \lor \ell_2 \lor y_{C,2}) \land (\lnot y_{C,2} \lor \ell_3 \lor y_{C,3}) \land \cdots \land (\lnot y_{C,k-2} \lor \ell_{k-1} \lor \ell_k),
 where the y_{C,i} are new variables. You can use that an assignment to the variables of C satisfies C if and only if it can be extended to the variables y_{C,i} so that it satisfies \tilde C.





Exercise 33.7 (\mathsf{NAE}\text{-}3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}) A 3-CNF formula is NAE-satisfiable (not-all-equal satisfiable) if there is an assignment under which every clause has at least one true literal and at least one false literal. Let 
\mathsf{NAE}\text{-}3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}= \{\, \langle  F \rangle :  F \text{ is a } 3\text{-CNF formula that is NAE-satisfiable} \,\}.
 Show that \mathsf{NAE}\text{-}3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete.






TipHint





Prove that \mathsf{NAE}\text{-}3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{NP} and construct a polynomial-time reduction showing that 3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}\leqslant_p \mathsf{NAE}\text{-}3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}.
First show that if an assignment a NAE-satisfies F, then so does its complement \bar a, defined by \bar a(x) = 1 - a(x) for every variable x.
For the reduction, take one new variable z shared by the whole formula. For each clause C = \ell_1 \lor \ell_2 \lor \ell_3, take a new variable y_C and let 
\tilde C = (\ell_1 \lor \ell_2 \lor y_C) \land (\lnot y_C \lor \ell_3 \lor z).
 You can use that an assignment with z = 0 satisfies C if and only if it can be extended to y_C so that it NAE-satisfies \tilde C. Use the complement property above to explain why you may assume z = 0.





Exercise 33.8 (\mathsf{1\text{-}in\text{-}3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}}) A 3-CNF formula is 1-in-3-satisfiable if there is an assignment under which every clause has exactly one true literal. Let 
\mathsf{1\text{-}in\text{-}3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}} = \{\, \langle \varphi \rangle : \varphi \text{ is a } 3\text{-CNF formula that is 1-in-3-satisfiable} \,\}.
 Show that \mathsf{1\text{-}in\text{-}3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}} is \mathbf{NP}-complete.






TipHint





Prove that \mathsf{1\text{-}in\text{-}3\text{-}SAT} \in \mathbf{NP} and construct a polynomial-time reduction showing that 3\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}\leqslant_p \mathsf{1\text{-}in\text{-}3\text{-}SAT}. For the reduction, take four new variables a_C, b_C, c_C, d_C for each clause C = \ell_1 \lor \ell_2 \lor \ell_3, and let 
\tilde C = (\lnot \ell_1 \lor a_C \lor b_C) \land (b_C \lor \ell_2 \lor c_C) \land (c_C \lor d_C \lor \lnot \ell_3).
 You can use that an assignment satisfies C if and only if it can be extended to a_C, b_C, c_C, d_C so that every clause of \tilde C has exactly one true literal.

title: 33  \mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete
text:
33.4 Variants of \mathtt{SAT} in \mathbf{P}
In this section we collect some (somewhat guided) exercises about variations of \mathtt{SAT} which do not remain \mathbf{NP}-complete, and actually are in \mathbf{P}.

Exercise 33.9 (2\mathtt{SAT}) Given a 2-CNF formula F, its implication graph G_F has one vertex for each literal x and \lnot x. Each clause (\ell_1 \lor \ell_2) adds the edges \lnot \ell_1 \to \ell_2 and \lnot \ell_2 \to \ell_1. A clause (\ell) with a single literal is treated as (\ell \lor \ell).

Show that F is unsatisfiable if and only if there is a variable x such that G_F has a path from x to \lnot x and a path from \lnot x to x.
Show that 2\mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P}.







TipHint





For a., every edge \ell \to \ell' of G_F means that in every satisfying assignment, if \ell is true then so is \ell'. This also holds along paths, which gives one direction. For the other direction, build an assignment step by step. Pick a literal \ell that has no value yet and such that there is no path from \ell to \lnot \ell. Set \ell and every literal reachable from \ell to true, and repeat. Show that this never makes both a literal and its negation true, and that every clause ends up satisfied.
For b., use that it can be decided in polynomial time whether a graph has a path between two given vertices (for example, by breadth-first search).





Exercise 33.10 (\mathsf{HORN}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}) A Horn clause is a clause with at most one positive literal, such as (\lnot x_1 \lor \lnot x_2 \lor x_3), (\lnot x_1 \lor \lnot x_4) or (x_2). A Horn formula is a CNF formula all of whose clauses are Horn clauses. Let 
\mathsf{HORN}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}= \{\, \langle F \rangle : F \text{ is a satisfiable Horn formula} \,\}.
 Show that \mathsf{HORN}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P}.






TipHint





A Horn clause (\lnot x_1 \lor \cdots \lor \lnot x_k \lor y) is equivalent to the implication x_1 \land \cdots \land x_k \to y. Consider the following algorithm. Start with all variables set to 0. While some clause is false, do the following:

if the false clause has a positive literal y, set y to 1;
otherwise, reject.

If no clause is false, accept. Show that every variable the algorithm sets to 1 is equal to 1 in every satisfying assignment of F, and use this to prove that the algorithm is correct. How many times can the loop run?





Exercise 33.11 (\mathsf{XOR}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}) An XOR clause is an expression \ell_1 \oplus \ell_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus \ell_k, where the \ell_i are literals and \oplus is exclusive or. It is true if and only if an odd number of its literals are true. An XOR formula is a conjunction of XOR clauses, encoded like a CNF formula with \oplus in place of \lor. Let 
\mathsf{XOR}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}= \{\, \langle F \rangle : F \text{ is a satisfiable XOR formula} \,\}.
 Show that \mathsf{XOR}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P}.






TipHint





Identify true with 1 and false with 0, and work in the field \mathbb{F}_2 = \{0,1\}, where addition is \oplus. Then \lnot x = 1 + x, so each XOR clause becomes a linear equation in the variables. For example, x_1 \oplus \lnot x_2 \oplus x_3 becomes x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0. So F is satisfiable if and only if a system of linear equations over \mathbb{F}_2 has a solution. Use Gaussian elimination, and count the number of operations it needs. Why does it matter for the running time that every number that appears is a single bit?





Exercise 33.12 (\mathsf{DNF}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}) A term is a conjunction of one or more literals. A formula in disjunctive normal form (DNF) is a disjunction of one or more terms, for example (x_1 \land \lnot x_2) \lor (\lnot x_1 \land x_2 \land x_3). DNF formulas are encoded like CNF formulas with the roles of \land and \lor swapped. Let 
\mathsf{DNF}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}= \{\, \langle F \rangle : F \text{ is a satisfiable DNF formula} \,\}.


Show that \mathsf{DNF}\text{-}\mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P}.
Every CNF formula is equivalent to a DNF formula (distribute \land over \lor). Explain why this does not show that \mathtt{SAT}\in \mathbf{P}.
Let F_n = (x_1 \lor y_1) \land (x_2 \lor y_2) \land \cdots \land (x_n \lor y_n). Show that every DNF formula equivalent to F_n has at least 2^n terms.







TipHint





For a., a DNF formula is satisfiable if and only if one of its terms is satisfiable. When is a single term satisfiable?
For b., think about how long the translation takes as a function of |\langle F \rangle|.
For c., for each S \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}, let a_S be the assignment that sets x_i = 1 and y_i = 0 for i \in S, and x_i = 0 and y_i = 1 for i \notin S. Let F' be a DNF formula equivalent to F_n, and let t be a term of F' satisfied by a_S. Show that t must contain x_i for every i \in S and y_i for every i \notin S. (If t is missing, say, x_i, change a_S by setting x_i = 0. Then t is still true but F_n is false.) Conclude that different sets S need different terms.

title: 33  \mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete
text: The values 0 and 1 play the role of the thruth values false and true respectively.↩︎

title: 34  \mathbf{NP}-complete problems on graphs
text:
34.1 Encoding of graphs
The first \mathbf{NP}-complete problems we have seen are about formulas. Many problems on graphs turn out to be just as hard. In this chapter we study two classic examples: finding a large clique, and coloring the vertices of a graph with few colors.
All graphs in this section are simple and undirected. A graph is a pair G = (V, E), where V = \{1, 2, \dots, n\} and E is a set of edges. Each edge is a set \{u, v\} of two distinct vertices u, v \in V.
We encode a graph by its adjacency matrix, the n \times n matrix A = (a_{uv}) with 
a_{uv} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \{u,v\} \in E, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
 We write A row by row over the alphabet \Sigma_G = \{\textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0}}, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{1}}, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}}\}, with a \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}} between rows: 
\langle G \rangle = a_{11} a_{12} \cdots a_{1n}\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}}\, a_{21} a_{22} \cdots a_{2n}\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}}\, \cdots\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#}}\, a_{n1} a_{n2} \cdots a_{nn}.
 A word over \Sigma_G encodes a graph if and only if it consists of n blocks of n bits each, and the matrix they form is symmetric with zeros on the diagonal. This can be checked in polynomial time. The encoding of a graph with n vertices has length n^2 + n - 1.
When a problem also takes a number k as input, we write it in binary after the graph: 
\langle G, k \rangle = \langle G \rangle\, \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{\#\#}}\, \mathrm{bin}(k).
Another natural encoding is the edge list: the number of vertices, followed by the list of edges, each written as a pair of vertices in binary. For sparse graphs, this is shorter than the adjacency matrix. However, we must write the number of vertices n in unary, or list every vertex. Otherwise, a graph with n vertices and no edges would have an encoding of length \mathcal{O}(\log n), while its adjacency matrix has length about n^2, which is exponentially longer.
As with formulas, the number k must be written in binary or another base b \geqslant 2, never in unary, unless we say otherwise. For \mathtt{CLIQUE} and \mathtt{COLORING} this makes no difference, because the only interesting values of k satisfy k \leqslant n. For problems with numbers in the input, such as \mathtt{SUBSET\text{-}SUM}, it matters a lot.

title: 34  \mathbf{NP}-complete problems on graphs
text:
Example 34.1 Let G be the graph with V = \{1,2,3,4\} and E = \{\{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\}, \{3,4\}\}. This is a triangle on 1, 2, 3, together with an extra edge from 3 to 4.






Figure 34.1



Its adjacency matrix is 
A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
 so \langle G \rangle = \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0110\#1010\#1101\#0010}} and \langle G, 3 \rangle = \textcolor{darkred}{\mathtt{0110\#1010\#1101\#0010\#\#11}}.



Exercise 34.1 Show that the two encodings (adjacency matrix and edge list with n written in unary) have polynomially related lengths, and each can be computed from the other in polynomial time. So it doesn’t matter which one we use when we ask whether a graph problem is in \mathbf{P}, in \mathbf{NP}, or \mathbf{NP}-complete.

title: 34  \mathbf{NP}-complete problems on graphs
text:
34.2 \mathtt{CLIQUE}
Let G = (V, E) be a graph. A clique in G is a set of vertices K \subseteq V in which every two distinct vertices are joined by an edge: \{u, v\} \in E for all distinct u, v \in K. A clique with k vertices is a k-clique. We define 
\mathtt{CLIQUE}= \{\, \langle G, k \rangle : G \text{ has a } k\text{-clique} \,\}.

Cliques model groups of objects that are all pairwise compatible, such as people who all know each other in a social network, or tasks that can all be done together.

Example 34.2 Let G be the graph from Example 34.1. The set \{1,2,3\} is a 3-clique, so \langle G, 3 \rangle \in \mathtt{CLIQUE}. The vertex 4 is not adjacent to 1 or 2, so G has no 4-clique and \langle G, 4 \rangle \notin \mathtt{CLIQUE}.

In \mathtt{CLIQUE}, the number k is part of the input, this is important, as the next exercise shows. \mathtt{CLIQUE} is hard only because k can grow with the size of the graph.

Exercise 34.2 Show that for each fixed constant k, the language \{\langle G \rangle : G \text{ has a } k\text{-clique}\} is in \mathbf{P}.


Theorem 34.1 \mathtt{CLIQUE} is \mathbf{NP}-complete.






NoteProof





\mathtt{CLIQUE}\in \mathbf{NP}. A certificate for \langle G, k \rangle is a set K of k vertices. A verifier checks that |K| = k and that \{u, v\} \in E for every pair of distinct u, v \in K. This takes O(k^2) lookups in the adjacency matrix, which is polynomial time.
\mathtt{CLIQUE} is \mathbf{NP}-hard. We show that 3\mathtt{SAT}\leqslant_p \mathtt{CLIQUE}. Let 
F = C_1 \land C_2 \land \cdots \land C_m, \qquad C_j = \ell_{j,1} \lor \ell_{j,2} \lor \ell_{j,3},
 be a 3-CNF formula. We construct a graph G_F and output \langle G_F, m \rangle.
Vertices. For every clause C_j and every position i \in \{1,2,3\}, the graph G_F has a vertex (j,i), labeled with the literal \ell_{j,i}. So G_F has 3m vertices, in m groups of three, one group per clause. If the same literal occurs in several clauses, each occurrence gets its own vertex.
Edges. Two vertices (j,i) and (j',i') are joined by an edge if and only if

they come from different clauses, that is, j \neq j', and
their literals are not complementary: it is not the case that one of them is x and the other is \lnot x.

Two literals are consistent if they are not complementary, which means that some assignment makes both of them true. So an edge joins two literals from different clauses that can be true at the same time. Figure 34.2 shows the three possible cases.






Figure 34.2: When two vertices of G_F are joined by an edge.



Running time. The graph G_F has 3m vertices. Each entry of its adjacency matrix is obtained by comparing two literals of F, which takes time polynomial in |\langle F \rangle|. So \langle G_F, m \rangle can be computed from \langle F \rangle in polynomial time.

Example 34.3 Consider 
F = \underbrace{(x_1 \lor x_2 \lor x_3)}_{C_1} \land \underbrace{(\lnot x_1 \lor \lnot x_2 \lor x_3)}_{C_2} \land \underbrace{(x_1 \lor \lnot x_2 \lor \lnot x_3)}_{C_3}.
 Figure 34.3 shows the graph G_F. There are no edges inside a group. Between two groups, all edges are present except those joining complementary literals. For example, x_1 in C_1 is not joined to \lnot x_1 in C_2.






Figure 34.3: The graph G_F for F = (x_1 \lor x_2 \lor x_3) \land (\lnot x_1 \lor \lnot x_2 \lor x_3) \land (x_1 \lor \lnot x_2 \lor \lnot x_3).




We now show that 
F \text{ is satisfiable} \iff G_F \text{ has an } m\text{-clique}.

(\Rightarrow) Let \alpha be a satisfying assignment. Every clause C_j contains at least one true literal under \alpha. Pick one such literal in each clause, and let K be the set of the corresponding m vertices, one from each group. Any two vertices of K come from different clauses. They are also consistent, because both of their literals are true under \alpha, and a literal and its negation cannot both be true. So every two vertices of K are joined by an edge, and K is an m-clique.

Example 34.4 Figure 34.4 shows this for the example above, with the assignment x_1 = 1, x_2 = 0, x_3 = 1.






Figure 34.4



The assignment x_1 = 1, x_2 = 0, x_3 = 1 makes x_1 true in C_1, \lnot x_2 true in C_2 and x_1 true in C_3. These three vertices form a 3-clique.

(\Leftarrow) Let K be an m-clique in G_F. There are no edges inside a group, so K contains at most one vertex from each group. Since K has m vertices and there are m groups, it contains exactly one vertex from each group. Let L be the set of literals labeling the vertices of K. Every two literals in L are joined by an edge, so they are consistent, and hence L never contains both x and \lnot x. So we can define an assignment \alpha that makes every literal in L true, giving any value to the variables that do not appear in L. Every clause C_j contains a literal of L, which is true under \alpha. Hence \alpha satisfies F.
Therefore 3\mathtt{SAT}\leqslant_p \mathtt{CLIQUE}. Since 3\mathtt{SAT} is \mathbf{NP}-complete, \mathtt{CLIQUE} is \mathbf{NP}-hard, and hence \mathbf{NP}-complete.




In the proof of Theorem 34.1 we built a graph from a formula: we constructed small subgraphs, called gadgets, that represent variables and clauses, and connect them so that the formula is satisfiable exactly when the graph has the required property. In the proof of Theorem 34.2 we will do the same, but with a different gadget.

title: 34  \mathbf{NP}-complete problems on graphs
text:
34.3 \mathtt{COLORING}
Let k \geqslant 1. A k-coloring of a graph G = (V, E) is a map c\colon V \to \{1, \dots, k\} such that adjacent vertices get different colors: c(u) \neq c(v) for every edge \{u, v\} \in E. We say G is k-colorable if it has a k-coloring, and for each fixed k we define 
k\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} = \{\, \langle G \rangle : G \text{ is } k\text{-colorable} \,\}.

Colorings model conflicts. Take the vertices to be exams, put an edge between two exams that share a student, and take the colors to be time slots. Then a k-coloring is an exam timetable with k slots in which no student has two exams at the same time. Register allocation in compilers and assigning frequencies to radio transmitters lead to the same kind of problem.

Example 34.5 Let G be the graph from Example 34.1. The map c(1) = 1, c(2) = 2, c(3) = 3, c(4) = 1 is a 3-coloring, so \langle G \rangle \in 3\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING}. The vertices of a clique must all get different colors, and the triangle \{1,2,3\} is a clique, so G has no 2-coloring and \langle G \rangle \notin 2\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING}.

The example uses a general fact.

Exercise 34.3 Show that if \langle G,k\rangle\in \mathtt{CLIQUE}, then \langle G\rangle\notin(k-1)\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING}. Show that the converse is false.

The hardness of k\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} depends on k:

1\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} is trivial: G is 1-colorable if and only if it has no edges.
2\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} \in \mathbf{P}. A graph is 2-colorable if and only if it is bipartite, and this can be checked with a breadth-first search.
3\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} is \mathbf{NP}-complete, and so is k\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} for every fixed k \geqslant 3.


Theorem 34.2 k\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} is \mathbf{NP}-complete.






NoteProof





3\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} \in \mathbf{NP}. A certificate for \langle G \rangle is a map c\colon V \to \{1,2,3\}. A verifier checks that c(u) \neq c(v) for every edge \{u,v\} \in E, which takes polynomial time.
3\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} is \mathbf{NP}-hard. We show that 3\mathtt{SAT}\leqslant_p 3\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING}. Let F = C_1 \land \cdots \land C_m be a 3-CNF formula with variables x_1, \dots, x_n. We build a graph G_F from three kinds of pieces.
1. The palette. G_F contains a triangle on three vertices \mathsf{T}, \mathsf{F}, \mathsf{B} (for true, false and base). In every 3-coloring, these three vertices get three different colors. So, after renaming the colors if necessary, we may assume that \mathsf{T} has color \mathsf{T}, \mathsf{F} has color \mathsf{F} and \mathsf{B} has color \mathsf{B}. We then say a vertex is true if it has color \mathsf{T}, and false if it has color \mathsf{F}.
2. Variable gadgets. For each variable x_i, G_F contains two vertices x_i and \lnot x_i, which form a triangle with \mathsf{B} (Figure 34.5). Since every literal vertex is adjacent to \mathsf{B}, it gets color \mathsf{T} or \mathsf{F}. Since x_i and \lnot x_i are adjacent, exactly one of them is true. So a 3-coloring of these vertices is the same thing as an assignment of the variables.






Figure 34.5: The palette and the variable gadgets for x_1, x_2, x_3, colored according to the assignment x_1 = 1, x_2 = 0, x_3 = 1.



3. Clause gadgets. These are built from an OR gadget. It has two input vertices a, b, three new vertices p, q, o forming a triangle, and the edges a - p and b - q. The vertex o is the output. The OR gadget behaves like the \lor of its inputs (Figure 34.6):

(i) In every 3-coloring in which a and b are both false, o is false. Indeed, p and q cannot have color \mathsf{F} (because of a and b), and they must differ, so \{p, q\} get the colors \{\mathsf{T}, \mathsf{B}\}. This leaves only \mathsf{F} for o.
(ii) If a or b is true, then any coloring of a and b can be extended to p, q, o with o true. Say a is true. Color p and q with \mathsf{F} and \mathsf{B}, in the order that gives q a different color from b, and color o with \mathsf{T}. The case where b is true is symmetric.







Figure 34.6: The OR gadget with inputs a, b and output o.



For each clause C_j = \ell_1 \lor \ell_2 \lor \ell_3, we add two OR gadgets, with 6 new vertices in total. The first computes o_1 = \mathrm{OR}(\ell_1, \ell_2), the second computes o_2 = \mathrm{OR}(o_1, \ell_3), and we add the edges o_2 - \mathsf{F} and o_2 - \mathsf{B}. These two edges force o_2 to be true (Figure 34.7). Here \ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3 are the literal vertices of the variable gadgets. So, unlike in the reduction to \mathtt{CLIQUE}, a literal that occurs in several clauses is a single vertex, shared by all of their gadgets.






Figure 34.7: The gadget for a clause \ell_1 \lor \ell_2 \lor \ell_3, colored for the case where \ell_1, \ell_2 are false and \ell_3 is true. The first OR gadget outputs false, but \ell_3 makes the second one output true, as required.



Running time. G_F has 3 + 2n + 6m vertices: the palette, two vertices per variable and six per clause. Moreover its edges are given by fixed patterns, so \langle G_F \rangle can be computed from \langle F \rangle in polynomial time.
We now show that 
F \text{ is satisfiable} \iff G_F \text{ is } 3\text{-colorable}.

(\Rightarrow) Let \alpha be a satisfying assignment. Color the palette with \mathsf{T}, \mathsf{F}, \mathsf{B}, and color each literal vertex \mathsf{T} or \mathsf{F} according to its value under \alpha. Now take a clause C_j = \ell_1 \lor \ell_2 \lor \ell_3.

If \ell_1 or \ell_2 is true, use (ii) to color the first OR gadget with o_1 true. Then use (ii) again to color the second OR gadget with o_2 true.
Otherwise \ell_3 is true. Color the first OR gadget with p_1 = \mathsf{T}, q_1 = \mathsf{B}, o_1 = \mathsf{F}, and use (ii) to color the second OR gadget with o_2 true.

In both cases o_2 has color \mathsf{T}, which is compatible with its edges to \mathsf{F} and \mathsf{B}. Different clause gadgets share only literal and palette vertices, which are already colored, so these colorings fit together into a 3-coloring of G_F.
(\Leftarrow) Take a 3-coloring of G_F, with the colors renamed so that the palette vertices have colors \mathsf{T}, \mathsf{F}, \mathsf{B}. As we saw above, every literal vertex is true or false, and x_i and \lnot x_i have different colors. Define \alpha(x_i) = 1 if and only if x_i has color \mathsf{T}. Then a literal is true under \alpha if and only if its vertex has color \mathsf{T}.
Suppose, for a contradiction, that some clause C_j has all three literals false. By (i), o_1 is false. Then both inputs of the second OR gadget are false, so by (i) again, o_2 is false. But o_2 is adjacent to \mathsf{F}, which is a contradiction (Figure 34.8). Hence every clause has a true literal, and \alpha satisfies F.






Figure 34.8: If all three literals are false, then o_1 and then o_2 are forced to be false. But o_2 is adjacent to \mathsf{F}, so no 3-coloring exists.



Therefore 3\mathtt{SAT}\leqslant_p 3\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING}, and 3\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} is \mathbf{NP}-complete.





Exercise 34.4 Show that k\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} is \mathbf{NP}-complete, for every k\geqslant 3.

title: 35  More exercises
text:
Important



The explanations of wrong anwers are partially generated using AI tools. Please report any error.



Exercise 35.1 (Brute force for triangles)  

Consider the problem \mathtt{TRIANGLEFREE}: given an undirected graph G, encoded as an adjacency matrix, decide whether G contains no triangle. A triangle is a set of three vertices u, v, w that are pairwise connected: \{u,v\}, \{v,w\}, \{w,u\} \in E(G). Let n = |V(G)|. What can we say about the algorithm that considers every set of three vertices and, for each one, checks whether they form a triangle?




A. It is \mathcal{O}(3n) = \mathcal{O}(n).


The algorithm looks at every set of three vertices, and there are \binom{n}{3} = \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6} of them. The 3 is the size of each set, not a factor in front of n. Since \binom{n}{3} grows like n^3/6, the algorithm is \mathcal{O}(n^3), not \mathcal{O}(n).




B. It is \mathcal{O}(n^3), but it is not clear how to decide \mathtt{TRIANGLEFREE} in linear time.


There are \binom{n}{3} = \mathcal{O}(n^3) sets of three vertices, and each one is checked with three lookups in the adjacency matrix, so the algorithm runs in time \mathcal{O}(n^3). The input is an n \times n matrix, so its size is N = n^2, and linear time means \mathcal{O}(n^2). The best known algorithms reduce triangle detection to matrix multiplication and take about \mathcal{O}(n^{2.37}). Whether time \mathcal{O}(n^2) is possible is an open problem.




C. It is \mathcal{O}(3^n), and it is not clear how to decide \mathtt{TRIANGLEFREE} in polynomial time.


The number of sets of three vertices is \binom{n}{3} \leqslant n^3, which is polynomial in n, not exponential. Exponentially many subsets appear only when the size of the subsets is part of the input, as in \mathtt{CLIQUE}. Here the size is fixed at 3, so the brute-force algorithm already runs in polynomial time.




D. None of the other answers is correct.


One of the other answers is correct. The algorithm checks \binom{n}{3} = \mathcal{O}(n^3) triples, each in constant time. Since the input has size n^2, linear time would mean \mathcal{O}(n^2), and no such algorithm is known.





Exercise 35.2 (From 3 colors to k colors)  

We want to show that 
3\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} \leqslant_m^p k\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING}
 for every k \geqslant 4. Which of the following ideas leads to a correct reduction? Given an undirected graph G as input, we build a graph G' consisting of




A. the disjoint union of G and a k-clique.


The k-clique can be colored with k colors on its own, and since it is not connected to G, it puts no constraint on G. So G' is k-colorable if and only if G is k-colorable, which is a different question from whether G is 3-colorable. For example, take k = 4 and G = K_4. Then G is not 3-colorable, but G' is 4-colorable, so the reduction maps a no-instance to a yes-instance.




B. the union of G and a k-clique, plus all possible edges between the copy of G and the k-clique.


The k-clique uses all k colors, and every vertex of G is adjacent to all of them. So, as soon as G has a vertex, G' contains a (k+1)-clique and is never k-colorable. The reduction maps every graph, including the 3-colorable ones, to a no-instance.




C. the disjoint union of G and a (k-3)-clique.


Since the (k-3)-clique is not connected to G, it does not restrict the colors available to G. So G' is k-colorable if and only if G is k-colorable, not 3-colorable. The same counterexample as before works: G = K_4 with k = 4 is not 3-colorable, but G' is 4-colorable.




D. the union of G and a (k-3)-clique, plus all possible edges between the copy of G and the (k-3)-clique.


The (k-3)-clique needs k-3 different colors, and every vertex of G is adjacent to all of them. So, in a k-coloring of G', the vertices of G can only use the 3 remaining colors, which gives a 3-coloring of G. Conversely, a 3-coloring of G together with k-3 new colors for the clique is a k-coloring of G'. Hence G \in 3\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING} \iff G' \in k\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING}, and G' can be built in polynomial time.





Exercise 35.3 (Equivalence classes in \mathbf{P})  

Since the relation \equiv_m^p is an equivalence relation, it divides the class \mathbf{P} into equivalence classes. How many?




A. 1


Not every language in \mathbf{P} is equivalent to every other. The language \emptyset only reduces to itself: if L \leqslant_m^p \emptyset, then w \in L \iff f(w) \in \emptyset, so L = \emptyset. In the same way, only \Sigma^* reduces to \Sigma^*. So \emptyset and \Sigma^* are each alone in their class.




B. 2


The two trivial languages \emptyset and \Sigma^* are not equivalent to each other, nor to any other language: the only language that reduces to \emptyset is \emptyset itself, and the only one that reduces to \Sigma^* is \Sigma^*. Together with the class of all the remaining languages in \mathbf{P}, this gives more than two classes.




C. 3


The classes are \{\emptyset\}, \{\Sigma^*\} and all the other languages in \mathbf{P}. If L_1, L_2 \in \mathbf{P} and L_2 \neq \emptyset, \Sigma^*, then L_1 \leqslant_m^p L_2: fix a word y \in L_2 and a word n \notin L_2, and let f(w) = y if w \in L_1 and f(w) = n otherwise. This f is computable in polynomial time, because the reduction can decide L_1 by itself. So all nontrivial languages in \mathbf{P} are equivalent. On the other hand, only \emptyset reduces to \emptyset and only \Sigma^* reduces to \Sigma^*.




D. \infty


Inside \mathbf{P}, polynomial-time reductions are too powerful to tell languages apart: a reduction can simply solve the instance and output a fixed yes-instance or a fixed no-instance. So all languages in \mathbf{P} other than \emptyset and \Sigma^* are equivalent, and there are only finitely many classes. (Finer distinctions inside \mathbf{P} need weaker reductions, for example reductions computable in logarithmic space.)





Exercise 35.4 (Isomorphic graphs)  

Which of the following graphs are isomorphic?





A. (a) and (b)


In graph (b), the vertices 6, 8 and 10 form a triangle. Graph (a) is the Petersen graph, which has no triangles (it has no cycles of length less than 5). An isomorphism maps triangles to triangles, so (a) and (b) are not isomorphic. Also, (b) has two vertices of degree 4, while every vertex of (a) has degree 3.




B. (c) and (d)


Graph (d) contains cycles of length 4, for example 1, 2, 7, 6. Graph (c) has no cycle of length less than 5. An isomorphism maps 4-cycles to 4-cycles, so (c) and (d) are not isomorphic, even though both have 10 vertices of degree 3 and 15 edges.




C. (a) and (c)


Both are drawings of the Petersen graph. The map 
1 \mapsto 1,\ 2 \mapsto 2,\ 3 \mapsto 3,\ 4 \mapsto 4,\ 5 \mapsto 10,\ 6 \mapsto 9,\ 7 \mapsto 8,\ 8 \mapsto 7,\ 9 \mapsto 6,\ 10 \mapsto 5
 sends every edge of (a) to an edge of (c), and both graphs have 15 edges, so it is an isomorphism. Note how different the two drawings look. In general, no polynomial-time algorithm for graph isomorphism is known, although it is not believed to be \mathbf{NP}-complete.




D. (b) and (d)


Graph (b) has a triangle (6, 8, 10), but graph (d) has none, so they are not isomorphic. Counting degrees also works: (b) has two vertices of degree 4, and every vertex of (d) has degree 3.





Exercise 35.5 (Subgraph isomorphism)  

The subgraph isomorphism problem, \mathtt{SGI}, is the following:

Given two graphs G and H, decide whether G contains a subgraph that is isomorphic to H.

What can we say about this problem?




A. It is equivalent to \mathtt{GI}.


\mathtt{GI} reduces to \mathtt{SGI}: two graphs with the same number of vertices and edges are isomorphic if and only if one is isomorphic to a subgraph of the other. But \mathtt{SGI} is \mathbf{NP}-complete, so if it reduced to \mathtt{GI}, then \mathtt{GI} would be \mathbf{NP}-complete too, which is believed to be false. So we cannot claim that the two problems are equivalent.




B. It is in \mathbf{P}.


\mathtt{SGI} is \mathbf{NP}-complete (see the correct answer), so it is in \mathbf{P} only if \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}. We cannot claim this.




C. It is \mathbf{NP}-complete.


\mathtt{SGI} \in \mathbf{NP}: a certificate is the subgraph of G together with the isomorphism, and both can be checked in polynomial time. It is \mathbf{NP}-hard because \mathtt{CLIQUE}\leqslant_m^p \mathtt{SGI}: map \langle G, k \rangle to \langle G, K_k \rangle, where K_k is the complete graph on k vertices. A subgraph of G isomorphic to K_k is exactly a k-clique in G. Unlike \mathtt{GI}, which is a candidate \mathbf{NP}-intermediate problem, \mathtt{SGI} is as hard as any problem in \mathbf{NP}.




D. None of the above.


One of the answers is correct: \mathtt{SGI} is in \mathbf{NP}, and \mathtt{CLIQUE} reduces to it by taking H = K_k, so it is \mathbf{NP}-complete.





Exercise 35.6 (Minimal formulas)  

Two Boolean formulas F and F' over n variables are equivalent if F(\alpha) = F'(\alpha) for every \alpha \in \{0,1\}^n. We define the problem 
\mathtt{MIN}\text{-}\mathtt{FRM} = \{\, \langle F \rangle : F \text{ is a Boolean formula with no smaller equivalent formula} \,\}.
 Which class can we guarantee that \mathtt{MIN}\text{-}\mathtt{FRM} belongs to?




A. \mathbf{NP}


To show that F is minimal, it is not enough to exhibit one object: we must rule out every smaller formula. A short certificate for “no smaller formula is equivalent” is not known. What is easy to certify is the opposite, that F is not minimal, and even that needs two quantifiers (see the correct answer).




B. \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}


The statement “for every smaller formula F', F' is not equivalent to F” starts with a universal quantifier, but “not equivalent” is itself an existential statement: there is an \alpha with F(\alpha) \neq F'(\alpha). So the definition has the form \forall F'\, \exists \alpha, with two quantifiers, and a single \forall followed by a polynomial-time check is not known to suffice.




C. \Sigma_2^p


It is the complement of \mathtt{MIN}\text{-}\mathtt{FRM} that is in \Sigma_2^p: F is not minimal if and only if \exists F'\, \forall \alpha\, \big[\, |F'| < |F| \text{ and } F'(\alpha) = F(\alpha) \,\big]. \mathtt{MIN}\text{-}\mathtt{FRM} itself has the form \forall\, \exists, and it is not known to be in \Sigma_2^p.




D. \Pi_2^p


By definition, 
\langle F \rangle \in \mathtt{MIN}\text{-}\mathtt{FRM} \iff \forall F'\ \exists \alpha\ \big[\, |F'| < |F| \Rightarrow F'(\alpha) \neq F(\alpha) \,\big].
 Both F' and \alpha have length at most |\langle F \rangle|, and the condition in brackets can be checked in polynomial time by evaluating both formulas. This is a \forall\, \exists statement followed by a polynomial-time check, so \mathtt{MIN}\text{-}\mathtt{FRM} \in \Pi_2^p.





Exercise 35.7 (Exact vertex cover (Partial exam 2, 05/06/2026))  

A vertex cover of a graph G is a subset of its vertices that includes at least one endpoint of every edge of G. Consider the \mathtt{EXACT\ VERTEX\ COVER} problem: “given a graph G and an integer k, is the minimum size of a vertex cover of G exactly k?”
With the theory seen in this course, you can prove that three of the following four statements are true. Which is the remaining one?




A. \mathtt{EXACT\ VERTEX\ COVER} \in \Sigma_1^p \cup \Pi_1^p.


This is the statement we cannot prove. “The minimum is exactly k” says two things: there is a vertex cover of size k, which is an \mathbf{NP} condition, and there is no vertex cover of size k-1, which is a \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP} condition. So the problem is the intersection of a language in \mathbf{NP}= \Sigma_1^p and a language in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}= \Pi_1^p. Nothing seen in the course shows that it is in \mathbf{NP} or in \mathbf{co}\mathbf{NP}, and this is believed to be false.




B. The complement of \mathtt{EXACT\ VERTEX\ COVER} belongs to \Pi_2^p.


This statement is true. \mathtt{EXACT\ VERTEX\ COVER} \in \Sigma_2^p: 
\langle G, k \rangle \in \mathtt{EXACT\ VERTEX\ COVER} \iff \exists C\ \forall C'\ \big[\, C \text{ is a vertex cover of size } k, \text{ and } C' \text{ is not a vertex cover of size } k-1 \,\big],
 and both conditions can be checked in polynomial time. Taking complements swaps \Sigma_2^p and \Pi_2^p, so the complement is in \Pi_2^p.




C. \mathtt{EXACT\ VERTEX\ COVER} \in \Sigma_3^p.


This statement is true. As shown in the previous option, \mathtt{EXACT\ VERTEX\ COVER} \in \Sigma_2^p, and \Sigma_2^p \subseteq \Sigma_3^p, because a verifier can ignore an extra certificate.




D. If \mathtt{EXACT\ VERTEX\ COVER} \notin \Sigma_1^p, then \Sigma_1^p \neq \Pi_1^p.


This statement is true. Consider the contrapositive: if \Sigma_1^p = \Pi_1^p, then the polynomial hierarchy collapses to \Sigma_1^p, so \Sigma_2^p = \Sigma_1^p. Since \mathtt{EXACT\ VERTEX\ COVER} \in \Sigma_2^p, it would then be in \Sigma_1^p.





Exercise 35.8 (Coloring planar graphs (Partial exam 2, 05/06/2026))  

Most computer scientists believe that \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}. Under this belief, one of the following statements is false. Which one?
Recall that all planar graphs are 4-colorable, and that a 4-coloring can be computed in polynomial time. Moreover, given a planar graph G, deciding whether G is 3-colorable is known to be \mathbf{NP}-hard.




A. There is some planar graph which is not 3-colorable.


This statement is true. The complete graph K_4 is planar (draw a triangle with one vertex in the middle, joined to the three corners), and it is not 3-colorable, because its four vertices are pairwise adjacent and need four different colors.




B. Given a graph G and a 4-coloring of it, deciding whether G is 3-colorable is a problem in \mathbf{P}.


This statement is false under the assumption \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}. The last option shows that this problem is \mathbf{NP}-hard. An \mathbf{NP}-hard problem in \mathbf{P} would give \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}. Knowing a 4-coloring does not help to find a 3-coloring.




C. Given a graph G with n vertices, deciding whether G is n-colorable is a problem in \mathbf{P}.


This statement is true, and the problem is trivial: every graph with n vertices is n-colorable, by giving each vertex a different color. So the algorithm always answers yes. This does not contradict the hardness of 3\text{-}\mathtt{COLORING}, because here the number of colors grows with the graph.




D. Given a graph G and a 4-coloring of it, deciding whether G is 3-colorable is \mathbf{NP}-hard.


This statement is true. We reduce 3-colorability of planar graphs, which is \mathbf{NP}-hard, to this problem. Map a planar graph G to the pair (G, c), where c is a 4-coloring of G. Since G is planar, c exists and can be computed in polynomial time. Clearly, G is 3-colorable if and only if (G, c) is a yes-instance.





Exercise 35.9 (A dichotomy for \mathbf{NP} (Partial exam 2, 05/06/2026))  

Suppose that every problem in \mathbf{NP} is either in \mathbf{P} or \mathbf{NP}-complete. Which of the following statements is true?




A. \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP} and \mathbf{NP}= \mathbf{EXP}


The two equalities together would give \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{EXP}. This contradicts the time hierarchy theorem, which shows that \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{EXP}, whatever we assume about \mathbf{NP}.




B. \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP} and \mathbf{NP}= \mathbf{EXP}


By Ladner’s theorem, if \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}, then there is a problem in \mathbf{NP} that is neither in \mathbf{P} nor \mathbf{NP}-complete. This contradicts the assumption, so \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP} is impossible here.




C. \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP} and \mathbf{NP}\neq \mathbf{EXP}


If we had \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP}, Ladner’s theorem would give an \mathbf{NP}-intermediate problem, contradicting the assumption. So \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}. Then \mathbf{NP}= \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{EXP} by the time hierarchy theorem. In general, \mathbf{P}\subseteq \mathbf{NP}\subseteq \mathbf{EXP} and at least one inclusion is strict. Here the assumption forces the first inclusion to be an equality, so the second must be strict.




D. \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP} and \mathbf{NP}\neq \mathbf{EXP}


By Ladner’s theorem, \mathbf{P}\neq \mathbf{NP} would imply the existence of an \mathbf{NP}-intermediate problem, contradicting the assumption that every problem in \mathbf{NP} is in \mathbf{P} or \mathbf{NP}-complete. So \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{NP}, and this option is false.
